chapters.title: Unit 11: The King and the Tamarind Drum

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. You sometimes meet or hear about a person who is very proud of his/her wealth, beauty or strength. What do you feel about such person?
    Ans: Such a person is vain and boastful. People do not respect a proud person, because he praises himself all the time and thinks only of himself. In this story the king was proud of his beauty, and his people grew poorer and sadder, yet he did not care about them.
  • Q: Q2. How do you wish someone could teach him/her a lesson?
    Ans: I wish such a person could be taught a lesson in a way that makes him realise his fault and change himself. Just as the king in this story was punished with horns and learnt humility in the forest, a proud person should learn that pride brings shame and that humility earns respect.

Explicit and Implied Meaning of the Story

  • Q: Q1. What is the explicit meaning of the story?
    Ans: If you praise yourself, people will think that you are boastful and will not respect you.
  • Q: Q2. What is the implied meaning of the story?
    Ans: Never be proud.

Glossary

  • Q: Give the meaning of 'vain'.
    Ans: Unsuccessful or of no value.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'courtiers'.
    Ans: A companion of a queen, king, or other ruler in their official home, especially in the past.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'boasted'.
    Ans: To speak too proudly or happily about what you have done or what you own.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'shriek'.
    Ans: A short, loud, high cry, especially one produced suddenly as an expression of a powerful emotion.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'fierce'.
    Ans: Physically violent and frightening.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'tamarind'.
    Ans: A type of tropical tree.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'turban'.
    Ans: A head covering for a man, worn especially by Sikhs, Muslims, and Hindus, made from a long piece of cloth that is wrapped around the top of the head many times.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'begged'.
    Ans: To make a very strong and urgent request.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'suntanned'.
    Ans: Pleasantly brown skin caused by being in hot sun.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'horns'.
    Ans: A hard, pointed, often curved part that grows from the top of the head of some animals.

Comprehension — A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. The king was a changed man after a long stay in the forest. List three changes in his character.
    Ans: Three changes in his character were: (1) he learnt to care for creatures smaller than himself; (2) he grew strong, wise and humble instead of vain and proud; and (3) he learnt about the beauty of the world around him and became a loving king.
  • Q: Q2. Why did his people grow poorer and sadder?
    Ans: The king spent more time having his hair combed in different styles and looking at himself in mirrors than in looking after his kingdom. He did not care about the welfare of his people, so as a result his people grew poorer and sadder.
  • Q: Q3. What was the barber's secret and why did he tell it to the tamarind tree?
    Ans: The barber's secret was that the king had horns on his head. He told it to the tamarind tree because he felt he would die if he did not tell someone and his stomach was bursting with the secret, but the king had warned that he would have him beaten and hanged if he talked about it to anyone, so he whispered it to the trunk of the tree instead of to a person.
  • Q: Q4. A fairy overheard the king calling himself more handsome than even the fairies. How did the fairy feel and what did he decide to do?
    Ans: The bad-tempered fairy was very angry when he heard the king's boast. He decided that something would have to be done about this king, and he planned to punish him by giving him horns, saying he would see how handsome the king would look with horns.
  • Q: Q5. What was the king's punishment?
    Ans: The king's punishment was that horns grew on his head, so that the handsome and vain king no longer looked handsome.
  • Q: Q6. Why did the king send for the royal barber early in the morning?
    Ans: When the king awoke and sat in front of his mirror, he found horns on his head and shrieked with horror. He sent for the royal barber immediately so that the barber could do something to cover up the horns.
  • Q: Q7. Why did barber cover his mouth with his hands when he saw the King?
    Ans: When the king slowly removed the pillow from his head, the barber saw the horns and clapped his hands to his mouth in horror and shock.
  • Q: Q8. What did the king say he would do if the barber talked about it?
    Ans: The king said that if the barber talked about the horns to anyone, he would have him beaten and hanged.

Comprehension — B. Put the statements in the correct sequence in which they happened

  • Q: Put in correct sequence: I am the most handsome king on Earth.
    Ans: Number 1 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: Loves only himself.
    Ans: Number 2 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: Does not care about the welfare of his people.
    Ans: Number 3 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: Boasts he is more handsome than even the fairies.
    Ans: Number 4 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: I am about to show you something, but if you talk about it to anyone.
    Ans: Number 5 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: 'Now go and tell the court I am unwell. I will not see anyone.'
    Ans: Number 6 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: I won't stay in the palace a moment longer.
    Ans: Number 7 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: Learns to love other creatures.
    Ans: Number 8 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: Is now kind and humble.
    Ans: Number 9 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: That day the king went down to a forest pool to drink water.
    Ans: Number 10 in the correct sequence.
  • Q: Put in correct sequence: Becomes a loving king and rules his people wisely.
    Ans: Number 11 in the correct sequence.

Comprehension — C. State whether each of the following is true or false

  • Q: 1. The people of the kingdom were proud of their king.
    Ans: False
  • Q: 2. The bad-tempered fairy decided to punish the king.
    Ans: True
  • Q: 3. The barber laughed when he saw the king's horns.
    Ans: False
  • Q: 4. The barber told the king's secret to the tamarind tree.
    Ans: True

Comprehension — D. Choose the best option to answer each question

  • Q: 1. Why did the bad-tempered fairy want to punish the king?
    Options: He heard the king say that he was as good-looking as the fairies. / He heard the king say that he looked better than all the fairies. / He heard the king say that he looked better than most fairies. / He heard the king say that he looked better than people of kingdom.
    Ans: He heard the king say that he looked better than all the fairies.
  • Q: 2. What did the king do when he found out that he had horns?
    Options: He asked for a new turban. / He chased everyone out of the room. / He called for the barber to cover his horns. / He called for the barber to cut his horns.
    Ans: He called for the barber to cover his horns.
  • Q: 3. Why did the king run off into the forest with the drum?
    Options: He wanted to destroy the drum. / He did so because the drum knew his secret. / He knew the drum would give him good advice. / He knew the drum would give him bad advice.
    Ans: He did so because the drum knew his secret.
  • Q: 4. How did life in the forest change the king?
    Options: He became a famous musician. / He became friends with the tree spirits. / He learnt to respect other living things. / He learnt to respect himself.
    Ans: He learnt to respect other living things.

mcqs.q: Why did the bad-tempered fairy want to punish the king?
options: He heard the king say that he was as good-looking as the fairies.
He heard the king say that he looked better than all the fairies.
He heard the king say that he looked better than most fairies.
He heard the king say that he looked better than the people of the kingdom.
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: the fairy overheard the king boast that he was more handsome than even the fairies, and decided to punish that pride.

mcqs.q: What did the king do when he found out that he had horns?
options: He asked for a new turban.
He chased everyone out of the room.
He called for the barber to cover his horns.
He called for the barber to cut his horns.
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: the king sent for the royal barber early in the morning so that the barber could do something to cover up the horns.

mcqs.q: Why did the king run off into the forest with the drum?
options: He wanted to destroy the drum.
He did so because the drum knew his secret.
He knew the drum would give him good advice.
He knew the drum would give him bad advice.
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: the drum made from the tamarind tree kept announcing that the king had horns, so the king fled with it because it knew his secret.

mcqs.q: How did life in the forest change the king?
options: He became friends with the tree spirits.
He learnt to respect other living things.
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: in the forest he learnt to care for creatures smaller than himself and grew strong, wise and humble.

mcqs.q: What is the explicit meaning of the story?
options: Never be proud of your wealth or strength.
If you praise yourself, people will think that you are boastful and will not respect you.
A king should always listen to his barber.
A drum can speak the truth about a king.
mcqs.why: The notes state the explicit meaning directly: if you praise yourself, people will think you are boastful and will not respect you.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'boasted' mean?
options: To make a very strong and urgent request
To speak too proudly or happily about what you have done or what you own
To give a short, loud, high cry
To grow a hard, pointed part on the head
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'boasted' as speaking too proudly or happily about what you have done or what you own, which is what the vain king did.

mcqs.q: Why did the king's people grow poorer and sadder?
options: Because a fierce storm blew down the tamarind tree.
Because the king spent more time having his hair combed and looking in mirrors than looking after his kingdom.
Because the barber told everyone the king's secret.
Because the fairy gave horns to all the people.
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the king cared only for his own looks and not for the welfare of his people, so his people grew poorer and sadder.

mcqs.q: What was the barber's secret?
options: That the king had horns on his head.
That the king was unwell and would see no one.
That the tamarind tree had been blown down.
That the king had run away to the forest.
mcqs.why: The barber's secret was that the king had horns on his head; he whispered it to the trunk of the tamarind tree because his stomach was bursting with it.

mcqs.q: What did the king say he would do if the barber talked about the horns to anyone?
options: He would make him the royal barber for life.
He would give him a new turban.
He would have him beaten and hanged.
He would send him to the forest.
mcqs.why: The king warned the barber that if he talked about the horns to anyone, he would have him beaten and hanged, which is why the barber told only the tree.

mcqs.q: Which of these statements about the story is true?
options: The people of the kingdom were proud of their king.
The barber laughed when he saw the king's horns.
The bad-tempered fairy decided to punish the king.
The barber kept the secret and told no one at all.
mcqs.why: The true/false exercise marks this statement True: the bad-tempered fairy was angry at the king's boast and decided to punish him by giving him horns.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary — A. Use dictionary to choose appropriate word definition and identify part of speech of the word

  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'rushing'.
    Ans: Meaning: moving very quickly; hurrying (as in 'They came rushing in'). Part of speech: verb.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'barber'.
    Ans: Meaning: a person whose job is to cut hair (the royal barber in the story). Part of speech: noun.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'trembling'.
    Ans: Meaning: shaking slightly, especially because of fear (as in 'a trembling finger'). Part of speech: verb.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'humble'.
    Ans: Meaning: modest; not proud. Part of speech: adjective.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'strong'.
    Ans: Meaning: having great power; not weak. Part of speech: adjective.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'palace'.
    Ans: Meaning: the official home of a king or queen. Part of speech: noun.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'surprise'.
    Ans: Meaning: a feeling of astonishment caused by something unexpected (as in 'he sat up in surprise'). Part of speech: noun.

Vocabulary — B. Find and underline the direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the text

  • Q: Find and underline the direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the text.
    Ans: The direct quotations in the story are: 'I am the most handsome king on Earth.' 'I am probably more handsome than all the fairies.' 'Something will have to be done about this king.' 'Horns!' 'I'll see how handsome the king will look with horns.' 'Out........out .....' 'Send for the royal barber immediately.' 'Barber, I am about to show you something, but if you talk about it to anyone, I will have you beaten and hanged.' 'Oh!' 'Well, don't just stand there.' 'Do something to cover them up.' 'Now go and tell the court I am unwell. I will not see anyone.' 'And remember my warning.' 'I'll die if I don't tell someone.' 'My stomach is bursting with the secret.' 'Let him make a drum from the trunk of the tamarind tree and play it outside my door.' 'The king has horns on his head. The king has horns on his head.' 'I won't stay in the palace a moment longer.' 'I'll go to the forest and live by myself.' 'Forgive him.' 'He has changed, remove his horns and give him back his kingdom.' 'Your Majesty, forgive us and come back, the kingdom needs you.'

Vocabulary — C. Rewrite five sentences from the story which have adjectives

  • Q: Rewrite a sentence from the story which has adjectives (Sentence 1).
    Ans: 'He was handsome but very vain.' The adjectives are 'handsome' and 'vain'.
  • Q: Rewrite a sentence from the story which has adjectives (Sentence 2).
    Ans: 'Unfortunately for the king a bad-tempered fairy happened to be flying by and was very angry when he heard this.' The adjective is 'bad-tempered' (and 'angry').
  • Q: Rewrite a sentence from the story which has adjectives (Sentence 3).
    Ans: 'The royal barber was a talkative little man.' The adjectives are 'royal', 'talkative' and 'little'.
  • Q: Rewrite a sentence from the story which has adjectives (Sentence 4).
    Ans: 'That night there was a fierce storm and the tamarind tree was blown down.' The adjective is 'fierce'.
  • Q: Rewrite a sentence from the story which has adjectives (Sentence 5).
    Ans: 'His lean, suntanned face looked back at him, without any horns!' The adjectives are 'lean' and 'suntanned'.

Vocabulary — D. Fill in the blanks with the adjectives given below (black, bitter, strong, warm, hot, difficult, long, hard, delicate)

  • Q: Coffee has a ______ taste, and people usually drink it with sugar or milk.
    Ans: bitter
  • Q: Some people like their coffee ______.
    Ans: black
  • Q: In Italy they drink very ______ black coffee.
    Ans: strong
  • Q: Some people drink their coffee with ______ milk.
    Ans: hot
  • Q: Coffee trees need sunshine and water, so they grow well in ______ countries.
    Ans: warm
  • Q: Coffee trees are very ______ and ______ to grow.
    Ans: delicate, hard
  • Q: Picking the beans is a ______ process.
    Ans: difficult
  • Q: The workers have a ______ job because they pick the beans by hand.
    Ans: difficult
  • Q: This can take a ______ time.
    Ans: long

Grammar — Sentences are given in the direct speech. Change them into the indirect speech

  • Q: 1. He said, 'I have got a toothache'.
    Ans: He said that he had got a toothache.
  • Q: 2. Manu said, 'I am very busy now'.
    Ans: Manu said that she was very busy then.
  • Q: 3. 'Hurry up,' she said to us.
    Ans: She ordered us to hurry up.
  • Q: 4. 'Give me a cup of water,' he told her.
    Ans: He asked her to give him a cup of water.
  • Q: 5. She said, 'I am going to college.'
    Ans: She said that she was going to college.
  • Q: 6. She said to me, 'Thank you'.
    Ans: She thanked me.

mcqs.q: What does 'rushing' mean, and what part of speech is it?
options: Moving very quickly; hurrying — a verb
Shaking slightly because of fear — a noun
Modest and not proud — an adjective
The official home of a king — a noun
mcqs.why: The notes give 'rushing' as moving very quickly or hurrying, as in 'They came rushing in', and its part of speech is a verb.

mcqs.q: What does 'barber' mean, and what part of speech is it?
options: A type of tropical tree — a noun
A person whose job is to cut hair — a noun
A head covering made of cloth — a verb
A feeling of astonishment — an adjective
mcqs.why: The notes define 'barber' as a person whose job is to cut hair — the royal barber in the story — and it is a noun.

mcqs.q: What does 'humble' mean, and what part of speech is it?
options: Pleasantly brown from the sun — a noun
mcqs.why: The notes give 'humble' as modest and not proud, the quality the king finally learnt in the forest, and it is an adjective.

mcqs.q: What does 'palace' mean, and what part of speech is it?
options: A short, loud, high cry — a verb
The official home of a king or queen — a noun
A companion of a ruler — an adjective
mcqs.why: The notes define 'palace' as the official home of a king or queen, the place the king said he would not stay in a moment longer, and it is a noun.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a direct quotation from the story, enclosed in quotation marks?
options: The king said that he was the most handsome king on Earth.
'I am the most handsome king on Earth.'
The king boasted about his good looks.
He was handsome but very vain.
mcqs.why: A direct quotation gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks; the notes list 'I am the most handsome king on Earth.' among the story's direct quotations.

mcqs.q: In the sentence 'He was handsome but very vain', which words are the adjectives?
mcqs.why: The notes point out that in this sentence from the story the adjectives are 'handsome' and 'vain', describing the king.

mcqs.q: In the sentence 'The royal barber was a talkative little man', which words are the adjectives?
mcqs.why: The notes identify 'royal', 'talkative' and 'little' as the adjectives in this sentence, all describing the barber.

mcqs.q: Fill in the blank with the correct adjective: 'Coffee has a ______ taste, and people usually drink it with sugar or milk.'
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with 'bitter': coffee has a bitter taste, which is why people usually drink it with sugar or milk.

mcqs.q: Fill in the blank with the correct adjective: 'Coffee trees need sunshine and water, so they grow well in ______ countries.'
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with 'warm', because coffee trees need sunshine and water and so grow well in warm countries.

mcqs.q: Fill in the blank with the correct adjective: 'Picking the beans is a ______ process.'
mcqs.why: The notes fill this blank with 'difficult': picking the coffee beans by hand is a difficult process that can take a long time.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I have got a toothache'.
options: He said that he has got a toothache.
He said that he had got a toothache.
He said that I have got a toothache.
He told that he will get a toothache.
mcqs.why: In indirect speech the present 'have got' moves back to 'had got' and 'I' becomes 'he', giving: He said that he had got a toothache.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: Manu said, 'I am very busy now'.
options: Manu said that she is very busy now.
Manu said that I am very busy then.
Manu said that she was very busy then.
Manu said that she will be very busy now.
mcqs.why: In indirect speech 'am' becomes 'was' and 'now' becomes 'then', giving: Manu said that she was very busy then.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: 'Hurry up,' she said to us.
options: She said to us that hurry up.
She ordered us to hurry up.
She asked us that we hurry up.
She said that she hurried up.
mcqs.why: A command in direct speech is reported with a verb like 'ordered' plus 'to': She ordered us to hurry up.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: 'Give me a cup of water,' he told her.
options: He told her that give him a cup of water.
He said her to give me a cup of water.
He asked her to give him a cup of water.
He ordered that she gives him water.
mcqs.why: This request is reported as: He asked her to give him a cup of water — 'me' changes to 'him' in indirect speech.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, 'Thank you'.
options: She said to me that thank you.
She says thank you to me.
She told me that she thanks.
mcqs.why: The notes report this simply as 'She thanked me', because 'said to me, Thank you' is summed up by the single verb 'thanked'.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — A. Write two paragraphs of comparison: the character of the king in the story 'The King and the Tamarind Drum'

  • Q: A. Write two paragraphs of comparison, the character of the king in the story 'The king and the Tamarind drum.' What sort of a person he was in the beginning of the story and after he ran away to the forest? Use appropriate similes for comparison and correct connectors of comparison.
    Ans: In the beginning of the story the king was handsome but very vain, and he was as proud as a peacock about his good looks. He looked at himself constantly in mirrors and in pools of water, and he spent more time having his hair combed in different styles than in ruling his kingdom. He loved only himself and did not care about the welfare of his people, so his people grew poorer and sadder. He was also cruel and short-tempered; for example, he threatened to have the barber beaten and hanged only for knowing his secret. In short, in the beginning he was selfish, boastful and unkind. After he ran away to the forest, however, the king became a completely different person. Whereas in the palace he had thought only of his own beauty, in the forest he gradually learnt about the beauty of the world around him. Unlike his former self, he learnt to care for creatures smaller than himself, and his only companion was the tamarind drum, which gave him good advice. He grew strong and wise and humble, and his lean, suntanned face no longer carried the pride of the old king. Finally, just as a student changes after a hard lesson, the king returned to his kingdom as a loving ruler and ruled his people wisely.

Writing — B. Write a story of your own on 'pride'

  • Q: B. Write a story of your own on 'pride'.
    Ans: Once there was a young horse in a village who was very proud of his speed. He would boast before all the other animals, 'No one in this valley can run as fast as I can.' He laughed at the old donkey who carried loads slowly, and he never helped anyone. One day the villagers arranged a race, and the proud horse was sure he would win. He ran carelessly, looking back again and again to enjoy the race, and he did not see a deep ditch in his way. He fell into the ditch and hurt his leg badly. No animal came forward at first, because he had always mocked them, but the kind old donkey slowly pulled a cart to the ditch and helped him out. The horse felt deeply ashamed of his pride. He thanked the donkey and promised never to boast again. From that day he used his speed to help others, carrying the sick and the weak to the town. Thus pride brought him a fall, but humility won him true friends and respect.

mcqs.q: Which simile is used for the king at the beginning of the story?
options: As wise as an owl about his kingdom
As proud as a peacock about his good looks
As kind as a loving ruler to his people
As quiet as a drum in the forest
mcqs.why: The comparison paragraph says the king in the beginning was as proud as a peacock about his good looks, a simile for his vanity.

mcqs.q: At the beginning of the story, the king spent more time on what than on ruling his kingdom?
options: Caring for creatures smaller than himself
Having his hair combed in different styles and looking at himself in mirrors
Walking in the forest and drinking at pools
mcqs.why: The notes say he looked at himself constantly in mirrors and in pools of water and spent more time having his hair combed than in ruling his kingdom.

mcqs.q: Which connector of comparison best fits: '______ in the palace he had thought only of his own beauty, in the forest he learnt about the beauty of the world around him.'
mcqs.why: 'Whereas' is the connector of comparison used in the paragraph to contrast the king's palace life with his changed life in the forest.

mcqs.q: What was the king's only companion in the forest?
mcqs.why: The notes say his only companion in the forest was the tamarind drum, which gave him good advice while he changed.

mcqs.q: After his stay in the forest, the king learnt to do what?
options: Comb his hair in more styles
Care for creatures smaller than himself
Punish anyone who knew his secret
Look at himself in pools of water
mcqs.why: Unlike his former self, the changed king learnt to care for creatures smaller than himself and grew strong, wise and humble.

mcqs.q: In the story written on 'pride', the young horse was proud of what?
mcqs.why: The horse in the story on pride was very proud of his speed and boasted that no one in the valley could run as fast as he could.

mcqs.q: What happened to the proud horse during the race?
options: He won the race easily and was praised by all.
He fell into a deep ditch and hurt his leg badly.
He stopped to help the old donkey win.
He ran to the town to carry the sick.
mcqs.why: Running carelessly and looking back again and again, the horse did not see a deep ditch, fell into it and hurt his leg badly.

mcqs.q: Who helped the proud horse out of the ditch?
options: The villagers who arranged the race
The kind old donkey he had always mocked
No one came to help him at all
mcqs.why: The kind old donkey, whom the horse had laughed at for carrying loads slowly, pulled a cart to the ditch and helped him out.

mcqs.q: How did the horse use his speed after he gave up boasting?
options: He raced every day to prove he was fastest.
He carried the sick and the weak to the town to help others.
He carried heavy loads like the old donkey.
He left the valley and lived alone.
mcqs.why: From that day the horse used his speed to help others, carrying the sick and the weak to the town, instead of boasting about it.

mcqs.q: What lesson does the horse's story teach at the end?
options: Speed is the greatest gift an animal can have.
A race should always be run looking back.
Pride brought him a fall, but humility won him true friends and respect.
Old animals should never be asked for help.
mcqs.why: The story ends with this moral: pride brought the horse a fall, but humility won him true friends and respect.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking

  • Q: Imagine you and your friend have just entered an examination hall and you have to give instructions to your friend about the rules to be observed there. He/she can ask you questions to clarify what you have said. (You can use: Don't bring in any papers or books into the hall; Write legibly; Read through your answers carefully; Be silent; Don't talk to your neighbour.)
    Ans: Model response: Me: Listen carefully. We have entered the examination hall, so first of all, be silent. Friend: Can I keep my notes with me for a last look? Me: No. Don't bring in any papers or books into the hall. Leave them outside. Friend: What should I do when I get the question paper? Me: Read the questions carefully, and write legibly so that the examiner can read your answers easily. Friend: Can I ask you if I do not understand a question? Me: No. Don't talk to your neighbour during the examination. Ask the teacher on duty instead. Friend: And what should I do at the end? Me: Read through your answers carefully before you hand in your paper, and check that you have written your roll number on it.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Predict the theme of the poem by looking at the picture.
    Ans: The pictures show mother animals with their young ones — a lioness with her cub, a koala with her baby and a penguin with her chick — so the theme of the poem can be predicted as a mother's love, care and hard work for her children. The poem 'Beautiful Hands' is about the loving, hard-working hands of a mother.

Reading — Deduce the meaning of the following words

  • Q: Deduce the meaning of 'beautiful'.
    Ans: Very pleasing to look at; lovely.
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of 'form'.
    Ans: The shape of something.
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of 'patient'.
    Ans: Able to work and wait calmly without complaining, even in difficulty.
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of 'fair'.
    Ans: Light in colour; pretty (in the poem, the hands were not fair at all).
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of 'sad'.
    Ans: Unhappy; sorrowful.

Glossary

  • Q: Give the meaning of 'such'.
    Ans: Used to add emphasis.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'scarcely'.
    Ans: Almost not / certainly not.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'hue'.
    Ans: A degree of lightness, darkness, strength, etc. of a colour.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'sculptor'.
    Ans: A person who has the art of forming solid objects that represent a thing, person, idea, etc. out of a material such as wood, clay, metal, or stone, or an object made in this way.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'wrinkled'.
    Ans: Having small lines on skin because of old age.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'weary'.
    Ans: Very tired, especially after working hard for a long time.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'toiling'.
    Ans: Hard work, especially work that makes you feel physically tired.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'distant'.
    Ans: Far away.

Comprehension — A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Who does the poetess praise in this poem?
    Ans: The poetess praises her mother, that is, her mother's beautiful hands, which worked hard for her children all her life.
  • Q: Q2. What words or phrases tell us that mother's hand are not pretty in the physical sense?
    Ans: The words and phrases are: 'They're neither white nor small', 'you, I know, would scarcely think that they were fair at all', and 'these ages wrinkled hands'. These show that the hands were not white, small or fair, and had become wrinkled with age.
  • Q: Q3. Why does the poetess praise the hands in the second stanza?
    Ans: In the second stanza the poetess praises the hands because, though her mother's heart was weary and sad, these patient hands kept toiling on so that the children might be glad. The hands rested not when the children were at their play; they worked without rest for the children's happiness.
  • Q: Q4. Who is the speaker in the poem?
    Ans: The speaker in the poem is the poetess herself, Ellen M. H. Gates. She is now grown up and, looking back to childhood's distant day, she lovingly remembers her own mother's hands.
  • Q: Q5. Write the main idea of the poem.
    Ans: The main idea of the poem is that a mother's hands are the most beautiful of all hands, not because they are white, small or fair, but because they work patiently and tirelessly, with love and sacrifice, to make her children happy.
  • Q: Q6. Why is the first word 'such' written in all capital?
    Ans: The first word 'SUCH' is written in all capitals for emphasis. The glossary also tells us that 'such' is used to add emphasis, so the capital letters stress how truly beautiful the mother’s hands are in the poetess's eyes.
  • Q: Q7. How can we pay back what our mother does for us?
    Ans: We can never fully pay back what our mother does for us, but we can try to return her love: we should respect and obey her, help her in the daily work of the house so that her hands may rest, care for her lovingly when she is old, tired or ill, and do our best to make her glad, just as her patient hands worked to make us glad.

Comprehension — B. Write the summary of the poem

  • Q: B. Write the summary of the poem.
    Ans: In the poem 'Beautiful Hands', the poetess Ellen M. H. Gates praises the hands of her mother. She says that these hands are neither white nor small, and no one would think them fair at all. She has seen other hands whose form and colour a sculptor might dream of, yet to her these old, wrinkled hands are the most beautiful of all. The reason is that, though her mother's heart was weary and sad, her patient hands kept toiling on so that her children might be glad. Looking back to the distant days of her childhood, the poetess almost weeps to think that those hands rested not while the children were at their play. Thus the poem teaches that the true beauty of a mother's hands lies in her love, patience and lifelong hard work for her children.

Reading Comprehension — Similes (Willow and Ginkgo)

  • Q: Read the poem aloud. Work in pairs and underline the similes. Underline all of the willow similes in one colour.
    Ans: The willow similes are: 1. 'The willow is like an etching' — the willow tree is compared to an etching, fine-lined against the sky. 2. 'The willow's music is like a soprano' — its music is delicate and thin like a soprano's voice. 3. 'The willow is sleek as a velvet-nosed calf' — the willow is compared to a velvet-nosed calf. 4. 'The willow's branches are like silken thread' — its branches are compared to silken thread.
  • Q: Read the poem aloud. Work in pairs and underline the similes. Underline all of the ginkgo similes in another colour.
    Ans: The ginkgo similes are: 1. 'Then ginkgo is like a crude sketch' — the ginkgo is compared to a crude sketch, hardly worthy to be signed. 2. 'The ginkgo's tune is like a chorus' — its tune is compared to a chorus with everyone joining in. 3. 'The ginkgo is leathery as an old bull' — the ginkgo is compared to an old bull. 4. 'The ginkgo's like stubby rough wool' — the ginkgo is compared to stubby rough wool.

mcqs.q: Whom does the poetess praise in the poem 'Beautiful Hands'?
options: A sculptor who dreams of beautiful forms
Her mother — her mother's beautiful hands
Other hands that are white and small
mcqs.why: The poetess Ellen M. H. Gates praises her mother, that is, her mother's beautiful hands, which worked hard for her children all her life.

mcqs.q: Which words show that the mother's hands were not pretty in the physical sense?
options: 'These ages wrinkled hands' — they were not white, small or fair and had wrinkled with age
'Patient hands kept toiling on' for the children
'Her heart was weary and sad' with worry
mcqs.why: The notes quote 'They're neither white nor small', 'scarcely think that they were fair at all' and 'these ages wrinkled hands' to show the hands were not physically pretty.

mcqs.q: Why does the poetess praise the hands in the second stanza?
options: Because they were white, small and fair.
Because a sculptor might dream of their form and colour.
Because, though her mother's heart was weary and sad, these patient hands kept toiling on so that the children might be glad.
Because they rested while the children were at their play.
mcqs.why: The second stanza praises the hands because they worked without rest, even though the mother's heart was weary and sad, so that her children might be glad.

mcqs.q: Who is the speaker in the poem?
options: One of the children at play
The poetess herself, Ellen M. H. Gates
mcqs.why: The speaker is the poetess herself, Ellen M. H. Gates, now grown up and looking back to childhood's distant day as she remembers her mother's hands.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'scarcely' mean?
mcqs.why: The glossary gives 'scarcely' as almost not or certainly not, as in the line that you would scarcely think the hands were fair at all.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'weary' mean?
options: Having small lines on the skin because of old age
Able to wait calmly without complaining
Very tired, especially after working hard for a long time
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'weary' as very tired, especially after working hard for a long time — the mother's heart was weary and sad, yet her hands kept toiling.

mcqs.q: Why is the first word 'SUCH' written in all capital letters?
options: Because it is the name of the poetess.
For emphasis — to stress how truly beautiful the mother's hands are.
Because every poem begins with a capital word.
Because it is a sculptor's name.
mcqs.why: The notes explain that 'SUCH' is in capitals for emphasis; the glossary also says 'such' is used to add emphasis.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a willow simile?
options: The willow is like an etching.
The ginkgo is like a crude sketch.
The ginkgo is leathery as an old bull.
The ginkgo's tune is like a chorus.
mcqs.why: The willow similes include 'The willow is like an etching', comparing the fine-lined tree against the sky; the other options are ginkgo similes.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a ginkgo simile?
options: The willow's music is like a soprano.
The willow's branches are like silken thread.
The ginkgo is leathery as an old bull.
The willow is sleek as a velvet-nosed calf.
mcqs.why: The ginkgo similes include 'The ginkgo is leathery as an old bull'; the other options compare the willow to a soprano, silken thread and a calf.

mcqs.q: What is the main idea of the poem?
options: A mother's hands are most beautiful when they are white, small and fair.
A sculptor can make the most beautiful hands of all.
A mother's hands are the most beautiful of all because they work patiently and tirelessly, with love and sacrifice, to make her children happy.
Children should play while their mother rests.
mcqs.why: The main idea in the notes is that the beauty of a mother's hands lies not in whiteness or fairness but in patient, tireless work done with love for her children.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar — A. Rewrite the sentences under SVO, DO and IO pattern

  • Q: 1. Arshad gave the dog a bone.
    Ans: Subject (S): Arshad; Verb (V): gave; Indirect Object (IO): the dog; Direct Object (DO): a bone. (Given in the book as the example.)
  • Q: 2. He sent us some foreign stamps.
    Ans: Subject (S): He; Verb (V): sent; Indirect Object (IO): us; Direct Object (DO): some foreign stamps.
  • Q: 3. The doctor gave her an injection.
    Ans: Subject (S): The doctor; Verb (V): gave; Indirect Object (IO): her; Direct Object (DO): an injection.
  • Q: 4. Sarah sent Palwasha a gift.
    Ans: Subject (S): Sarah; Verb (V): sent; Indirect Object (IO): Palwasha; Direct Object (DO): a gift.
  • Q: 5. She offered me a firm hand shake.
    Ans: Subject (S): She; Verb (V): offered; Indirect Object (IO): me; Direct Object (DO): a firm hand shake.
  • Q: 6. They sold him pictures.
    Ans: Subject (S): They; Verb (V): sold; Indirect Object (IO): him; Direct Object (DO): pictures.

Grammar — B. Identify whether the words in bold are used as direct objects or indirect objects

  • Q: 1. In the sentence 'She sent her friend a letter', is the bold word 'her friend' a direct object or an indirect object?
    Ans: Indirect object. ('Her friend' is the person to whom the letter was sent; 'a letter' is the direct object.)
  • Q: 2. In the sentence 'Sadaf will help you with your school homework', is the bold word 'you' a direct object or an indirect object?
    Ans: Direct object. ('You' is the person directly affected by the action of helping.)
  • Q: 3. In the sentence 'I need your help', is the bold word 'your help' a direct object or an indirect object?
    Ans: Direct object. ('Your help' is the thing that is needed.)
  • Q: 4. In the sentence 'He gave them a bag full of money', is the bold word 'them' a direct object or an indirect object?
    Ans: Indirect object. ('Them' are the people to whom the bag was given; 'a bag full of money' is the direct object.)
  • Q: 5. In the sentence 'Javed sold me his car', is the bold word 'his car' a direct object or an indirect object?
    Ans: Direct object. ('His car' is the thing that was sold; 'me' is the indirect object.)

mcqs.q: In 'Arshad gave the dog a bone', what is 'the dog'?
mcqs.why: In the SVO pattern given in the book's example, Arshad is the subject, 'gave' the verb, 'the dog' the indirect object and 'a bone' the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'He sent us some foreign stamps', what is the direct object?
mcqs.why: The pattern is S: He, V: sent, IO: us, DO: some foreign stamps — the stamps are the thing sent, so they are the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'The doctor gave her an injection', what is 'her'?
mcqs.why: 'Her' is the person to whom the injection was given, so it is the indirect object; 'an injection' is the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'Sarah sent Palwasha a gift', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: The pattern is S: Sarah, V: sent, IO: Palwasha, DO: a gift — Sarah does the action, so she is the subject.

mcqs.q: In 'She offered me a firm hand shake', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: The pattern is S: She, V: offered, IO: me, DO: a firm hand shake — 'offered' is the action word, the verb.

mcqs.q: In 'They sold him pictures', what is the direct object?
mcqs.why: The pattern is S: They, V: sold, IO: him, DO: pictures — the pictures are the thing sold, so they are the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'She sent her friend a letter', 'her friend' is:
options: A direct object, because it is the thing sent
An indirect object, because it is the person to whom the letter was sent
mcqs.why: The notes explain that 'her friend' is the indirect object because she is the person to whom the letter was sent; 'a letter' is the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'Sadaf will help you with your school homework', 'you' is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark 'you' as the direct object because 'you' is the person directly affected by the action of helping.

mcqs.q: In 'I need your help', 'your help' is:
mcqs.why: The notes mark 'your help' as the direct object because it is the thing that is needed in the sentence 'I need your help'.

mcqs.q: In 'He gave them a bag full of money', 'them' is:
mcqs.why: The notes explain that 'them' is the indirect object — the people to whom the bag was given — while 'a bag full of money' is the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'Javed sold me his car', 'his car' is:
options: A direct object, because it is the thing that was sold
An indirect object, because it is the person sold to
mcqs.why: The notes mark 'his car' as the direct object because it is the thing that was sold; 'me' is the indirect object.

mcqs.q: In 'Arshad gave the dog a bone', what is the verb?
mcqs.why: In the book's example pattern, 'gave' is the verb (V) — the action Arshad performs — with 'the dog' as indirect object and 'a bone' as direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'He sent us some foreign stamps', what is the subject?
mcqs.why: In this pattern the subject (S) is 'He', the one who does the sending; 'us' is the indirect object and 'some foreign stamps' the direct object.

mcqs.q: In 'The doctor gave her an injection', what is the direct object?
mcqs.why: The direct object (DO) is 'an injection', the thing given; 'her' is the indirect object and 'The doctor' is the subject.

mcqs.q: In 'They sold him pictures', what is 'him'?
mcqs.why: 'Him' is the indirect object — the person to whom the pictures were sold — while 'pictures' is the direct object and 'They' the subject.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Brainstorm: mind map titled 'mother'

  • Q: 'Brainstorm' to complete a list of ways that reflect how your mother worked restlessly in spite of facing problems of life, so that her family might enjoy a happy life. List your responses in mind map titled 'mother'.
    Ans: Mind map — 'mother' (ways my mother worked restlessly in spite of the problems of life, so that her family might enjoy a happy life): • She woke up early and worked till late at night without rest. • She cooked food for the whole family every day. • She washed the clothes and cleaned the house. • She cared for the children when they were ill and stayed awake at night with them. • She never rested while the children played, like the mother in the poem whose hands kept toiling on. • She faced the problems of life bravely and never let the family feel them. • She gave up her own comforts and wishes for the happiness of her family. • Even when her heart was weary and sad, her patient hands kept working so that her children might be glad.

mcqs.q: In the mind map titled 'mother', how did the mother begin and end her working day?
options: She woke up late and rested till night.
She woke up early and worked till late at night without rest.
She worked only while the children were at school.
She rested first and worked only in the evening.
mcqs.why: The mind map lists that she woke up early and worked till late at night without rest, working restlessly for her family.

mcqs.q: Which daily work of the mother is listed in the mind map?
options: She cooked food for the whole family every day.
She taught the children at school every day.
She sold food in the market every day.
She travelled to a distant town every day.
mcqs.why: The mind map records that she cooked food for the whole family every day, one of the ways she worked restlessly for a happy family life.

mcqs.q: Which household work is listed in the mind map?
options: She repaired the roof and painted the walls.
She washed the clothes and cleaned the house.
She guarded the house at night.
She drove the children to their play.
mcqs.why: The mind map lists that she washed the clothes and cleaned the house as part of her restless daily work for the family.

mcqs.q: What did the mother do when the children were ill?
options: She sent them to a distant hospital alone.
She rested and let them care for themselves.
She cared for them and stayed awake at night with them.
She called a sculptor to help them.
mcqs.why: The mind map says she cared for the children when they were ill and stayed awake at night with them, giving up her own rest.

mcqs.q: Like the mother in the poem, what did she never do while the children played?
options: She never rested — her hands kept toiling on.
She never let them feel happy.
She never faced the problems of life.
mcqs.why: The mind map links to the poem: she never rested while the children played, like the mother whose hands kept toiling on so the children might be glad.

mcqs.q: How did the mother face the problems of life, according to the mind map?
options: She faced them bravely and never let the family feel them.
She left them for the children to solve.
She complained about them all day.
She stopped working whenever they came.
mcqs.why: The mind map says she faced the problems of life bravely and never let the family feel them, so that the family might enjoy a happy life.

mcqs.q: What did the mother give up for the happiness of her family?
options: Her daily work in the house
mcqs.why: The mind map lists that she gave up her own comforts and wishes for the happiness of her family, a clear sign of her selfless love.

mcqs.q: Even when her heart was weary and sad, what did her patient hands do?
options: They rested at last while the children played.
They kept working so that her children might be glad.
They stopped toiling for the family.
They became white, small and fair.
mcqs.why: The mind map repeats the poem's thought: even when her heart was weary and sad, her patient hands kept working so that her children might be glad.

mcqs.q: What title is given to the mind map in this writing task?
mcqs.why: The brainstorming task asks for the responses to be listed in a mind map titled 'mother', showing the ways a mother works restlessly for her family.

mcqs.q: For what purpose did the mother work restlessly in spite of the problems of life?
options: So that she might become famous
So that a sculptor might praise her hands
So that she might rest in her old age
So that her family might enjoy a happy life
mcqs.why: The task itself states the purpose: she worked restlessly in spite of facing problems of life so that her family might enjoy a happy life.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. Who is the National poet of Pakistan?
    Ans: Allama Iqbal is the National Poet of Pakistan. The Pakistan government officially named him as the "The National Poet" and the "Ideological Founder of Pakistan".
  • Q: Q2. Have you read or heard his poetry?
    Ans: Yes, I have heard his poetry. He wrote poetry in Urdu and Persian. His famous Urdu collections are Bang-e-Dara (1924), Bal-e-Jibrael (1935) and Zarb-e-Kaleem (1936), and his Tarana-e-Hind is widely used in India as a patriotic song.

Glossary

  • Q: Give the meaning of: practice
    Ans: something that is usually or regularly done, often as a habit, tradition, or custom
  • Q: Give the meaning of: barrister
    Ans: a lawyer, who can give specialized legal advice and can argue a case in both higher and lower courts
  • Q: Give the meaning of: philosophical
    Ans: the use of reason in understanding such things as the nature of the real world and existence, the use and limits of knowledge, and the principles of moral judgment
  • Q: Give the meaning of: inspiration
    Ans: someone or something that gives you ideas for doing something
  • Q: Give the meaning of: voluminous
    Ans: piece of long and detailed writing
  • Q: Give the meaning of: mystic
    Ans: someone who attempts to be united with God through prayer
  • Q: Give the meaning of: commemorated
    Ans: to remember officially and give respect to a great person or event, especially by a public ceremony or by making a statue or special building
  • Q: Give the meaning of: ideological
    Ans: based on or relating to a particular set of ideas or beliefs
  • Q: Give the meaning of: communal
    Ans: belonging to or used by a group of people rather than one single person
  • Q: Give the meaning of: harmony
    Ans: a situation in which people are peaceful and agree with each other, or when things seem right or suitable together
  • Q: Give the meaning of: moralist
    Ans: a person who tries to force or teach other people to behave in ways he or she considers to be most correct and honest
  • Q: Give the meaning of: condolence
    Ans: sympathy and sadness for the family or close friends of a person who has recently died, or an expression of this, especially in written form
  • Q: Give the meaning of: reformer
    Ans: someone who tries to improve a system or law by changing it
  • Q: Give the meaning of: ultimately
    Ans: finally, after a series of things have happened
  • Q: Give the meaning of: youth
    Ans: young people, both male and female, considered as a group
  • Q: Give the meaning of: focused
    Ans: giving a lot of attention to one particular thing

Comprehension — A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Why is Allama Iqbal known as Dr. Mohammad Iqbal?
    Ans: Allama Iqbal is known as Dr. Mohammad Iqbal because he took his Doctorate Degree from Munich. He had done his M.A in philosophy in 1899, and after his doctorate he was called "Dr", which is one of his titles along with "Sir" and "Allama".
  • Q: Q2. Write about Iqbal's contribution in different fields?
    Ans: Iqbal contributed in many fields. In poetry, he wrote in Urdu and Persian and left valuable and voluminous treasures of poetry and prose, such as Israr-e-Khudi, Bang-e-Dara and Bal-e-Jibrael. In philosophy, he did his M.A and doctorate and wrote 'The Reconstruction of Religious Thoughts in Islam'. In law, he took his Barrister's Degree from London in 1908 and started practice as a Barrister. In politics, he joined the London branch of the All-India Muslim League and delivered the Allahabad Address in 1930. He was also a great moralist, a reformer and an educationist.
  • Q: Q3. What were the results of Allama Iqbal's efforts?
    Ans: As a result of Allama Iqbal's efforts, the Muslims of India woke from their sleep. In his Allahabad Address of December 1930, he pushed for the creation of a Muslim state in Northwest India, and he is regarded in Pakistan as the ideological founder of the state. The Pakistan government officially named him the "Ideological Founder of Pakistan".
  • Q: Q4. Why did Allama Iqbal want a separate state for the Muslims of India?
    Ans: Allama Iqbal wanted a separate state because he held that Muslims and Hindus are two major nations by any definition or test of a nation, and the two communities would not put their hearts in any venture together. So, in his Allahabad Address in 1930, he pushed for the creation of a separate Muslim state in Northwest India where the Muslims could live according to their own ideas and beliefs.
  • Q: Q5. What can the youth of today do to keep Allama Iqbal's dream alive?
    Ans: Allama Iqbal was deeply concerned about the youth. He was aware of the fact that if the youth focus on their self-realization then they can explore and achieve limitless skies. So the youth of today should focus on self-realization, work hard and follow his message to keep his dream alive.

Comprehension — B. State whether the following statements are true or false

  • Q: Allama Iqbal is known as a great novelist.
    Ans: False
  • Q: Allama Iqbal could not see the creation of Pakistan although he worked very hard for its creation.
    Ans: True
  • Q: In 1930, Quaid-e-Azam presided over the Allahabad meeting of the All India Muslim League
    Ans: False
  • Q: Allama Iqbal, the poet of the East, was born in Sialkot on 9th November 1877.
    Ans: True
  • Q: Allama Iqbal's efforts woke the Muslims from their sleep.
    Ans: True

Comprehension — C. Choose the correct option

  • Q: ______ is not Iqbal's poetic works.
    Options: Israr-e-Khudi / Ramuz-e-Bekhudi / Paigham-e-Mashriq / Zikr-e-Mir
    Ans: Zikr-e-Mir
  • Q: Allama Iqbal was known as ______
    Options: Poet of the East / Saint of the East / Writer of the East / Sufi of the East
    Ans: Poet of the East
  • Q: Most of Iqbal's work is in ______
    Options: Urdu / Persian / Punjabi / Arabic
    Ans: Persian

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT one of Iqbal's poetic works?
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: Israr-e-Khudi, Ramuz-e-Bekhudi and Paigham-e-Mashriq are Iqbal's works, while Zikr-e-Mir is not.

mcqs.q: Allama Iqbal was known as ______.
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: Allama Iqbal is known as the Poet of the East, and the true/false exercise uses the same title for him.

mcqs.q: Most of Iqbal's work is in ______.
mcqs.why: This is the book's own MCQ and key: Iqbal wrote in Urdu and Persian, but most of his work is in Persian.

mcqs.q: Which two titles did the Pakistan government officially give Allama Iqbal?
options: Poet of the East and Saint of the East
The National Poet and the Ideological Founder of Pakistan
Dr. Mohammad Iqbal and Sir Mohammad Iqbal
mcqs.why: The pre-reading notes say the Pakistan government officially named him 'The National Poet' and the 'Ideological Founder of Pakistan'.

mcqs.q: Which of these statements is true?
options: Allama Iqbal is known as a great novelist.
In 1930, Quaid-e-Azam presided over the Allahabad meeting of the All India Muslim League.
Allama Iqbal, the poet of the East, was born in Sialkot on 9th November 1877.
Allama Iqbal lived to see the creation of Pakistan.
mcqs.why: The true/false exercise marks this statement True; the novelist statement and the Quaid-e-Azam presiding statement are marked False, and Iqbal could not see Pakistan's creation.

mcqs.q: Why is Allama Iqbal known as Dr. Mohammad Iqbal?
options: Because he did his M.A in philosophy in 1899.
Because he took his Doctorate Degree from Munich.
Because he took his Barrister's Degree from London.
Because he joined the Muslim League in London.
mcqs.why: The notes say he is called 'Dr' because he took his Doctorate Degree from Munich; his M.A in philosophy, done in 1899, is a separate degree.

mcqs.q: In which field did Iqbal qualify in London in 1908?
options: Philosophy — he wrote on religious thought.
Law — he took his Barrister's Degree and started practice as a Barrister.
Politics — he delivered the Allahabad Address.
mcqs.why: The contribution notes say that in law he took his Barrister's Degree from London in 1908 and started practice as a Barrister.

mcqs.q: What did Iqbal push for in his Allahabad Address of December 1930?
options: The creation of a Muslim state in Northwest India
A united state for Muslims and Hindus together
The London branch of the Muslim League
A new collection of Persian poetry
mcqs.why: The notes say that in his Allahabad Address of 1930 he pushed for the creation of a Muslim state in Northwest India, which is why he is regarded as Pakistan's ideological founder.

mcqs.q: Why did Allama Iqbal want a separate state for the Muslims of India?
options: Because he wanted to become its first ruler.
Because he held that Muslims and Hindus are two major nations and the two communities would not put their hearts in any venture together.
Because his poetry was not read in India.
Because the Muslims of India were asleep and sad.
mcqs.why: The notes give his reason: Muslims and Hindus are two major nations by any test of a nation, so Muslims needed a state where they could live by their own ideas and beliefs.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'barrister' mean?
options: Someone who attempts to be united with God through prayer
A person who tries to improve a system or law by changing it
A lawyer who can give specialized legal advice and argue a case in both higher and lower courts
Someone or something that gives you ideas for doing something
mcqs.why: The glossary defines a barrister as a lawyer who can give specialized legal advice and argue a case in both higher and lower courts — Iqbal himself was one.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary — A. Find the meaning of the following words in a dictionary and locate entry words

  • Q: Give the dictionary meaning of: humour
    Ans: the quality of being funny or amusing; the ability to find things funny.
  • Q: Give the dictionary meaning of: wisdom
    Ans: the knowledge and good judgment that come from experience; the quality of being wise.
  • Q: Give the dictionary meaning of: famous
    Ans: known about by many people; well-known.
  • Q: Give the dictionary meaning of: struggle
    Ans: a hard effort to do or achieve something; to try very hard to deal with a difficulty.
  • Q: Give the dictionary meaning of: presided
    Ans: was in charge of a meeting or an event; led a formal meeting.

Vocabulary — B. Find five nouns from the lesson. Then change those nouns into adjectives

  • Q: Change the noun into an adjective: poetry
    Ans: poetic
  • Q: Change the noun into an adjective: religion
    Ans: religious
  • Q: Change the noun into an adjective: nation
    Ans: national
  • Q: Change the noun into an adjective: education
    Ans: educational
  • Q: Change the noun into an adjective: fame
    Ans: famous

Grammar — A. Add the ending punctuation marks in boxes and tell what kind of sentences these are: declarative, interrogative, imperative or exclamatory

  • Q: Q1. Alas __ I have lost the contest __ — Add the ending punctuation marks and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: Alas! I have lost the contest. — Exclamatory sentence.
  • Q: Q2. I need you to sit down now __ — Add the ending punctuation mark and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: I need you to sit down now. — Imperative sentence.
  • Q: Q3. It is too dangerous to climb that mountain __ — Add the ending punctuation mark and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: It is too dangerous to climb that mountain. — Declarative sentence.
  • Q: Q4. Do you know what the weather will be tomorrow __ — Add the ending punctuation mark and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: Do you know what the weather will be tomorrow? — Interrogative sentence.
  • Q: Q5. My mother makes delicious cookies __ — Add the ending punctuation mark and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: My mother makes delicious cookies. — Declarative sentence.
  • Q: Q6. Bravo __ we have won the match __ — Add the ending punctuation marks and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: Bravo! We have won the match. — Exclamatory sentence.
  • Q: Q7. O, that I could fly in the sky __ — Add the ending punctuation mark and tell what kind of sentence it is.
    Ans: O, that I could fly in the sky! — Exclamatory sentence.

Grammar — B. Choose the correct option

  • Q: 1. Which sentence is imperative?
    Options: The players were nervous before the game. / Kareem went to school for study. / Move the chairs into that corner quickly.
    Ans: Move the chairs into that corner quickly.
  • Q: 2. Which sentence is declarative?
    Options: May I have a clean plate? / I found my keys on the desk. / When will the store open today?
    Ans: I found my keys on the desk.
  • Q: 3. Which sentence is exclamatory?
    Options: Javaid used a towel to clean his hands. / I was tempted to take the last piece of cake. / Hurray! I won the match.
    Ans: Hurray! I won the match.
  • Q: 4. Which sentence is declarative?
    Options: What is your name? / Who told you this? / She is a successful writer.
    Ans: She is a successful writer.

Grammar — Punctuation Marks

  • Q: What is the full stop (.) used for?
    Ans: The full stop (.) is used to end all sentences except questions and exclamations, and after abbreviations for titles, names, and degrees, e.g. P.M. (Prime Minister), M.A, Ph.D.
  • Q: What is the question mark (?) used for?
    Ans: The question mark (?) is used to end a direct question, e.g. How are you?
  • Q: What is the exclamation mark (!) used for?
    Ans: The exclamation mark (!) is used after exclamations showing grief, joy, surprise, etc., e.g. How wonderful! What a terrible thing to happen!
  • Q: What is the comma (,) used for?
    Ans: The comma (,) is used to indicate a short pause and as a separator, always within the sentence, never at its end. It is used to separate words in a list, e.g. I have brought carrots, potatoes, and onions.
  • Q: What is the colon (:) used for?
    Ans: The colon (:) is used before a list, e.g. There are three things on the shopping list: rice, fruit, and biscuits.
  • Q: What is the dash used for?
    Ans: The dash is used to mark a break in a sentence, e.g. She wanted nothing more than peace — but even that could not be given to her.
  • Q: What is the hyphen (-) used for?
    Ans: The hyphen (-) is half the length of a dash and is used in compound words, e.g. mother-in-law, brother-in-law, out-of-town.
  • Q: What are quotation marks used for?
    Ans: Quotation marks are used to enclose a quotation, e.g. She said, "We must hurry now." They are also used before a short quotation.
