mcqs.q: Choose the correct determiner: '______ childhood is spent in terrible conditions.'
mcqs.why: The solved determiner exercise fills this blank with 'Their', referring to the child labourers whose childhood is spent in terrible conditions.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar — A. Add parentheses to enclose supplemental information, acronyms and dates or letters and/or numbers in a series

  • Q: Q1. She paid a lot Rs. 5000 for the cricket bat.
    Ans: She paid a lot (Rs. 5000) for the cricket bat. (Done in the book as the example.)
  • Q: Q2. His imprisonment lasted for four years 2002–2006.
    Ans: His imprisonment lasted for four years (2002–2006).
  • Q: Q3. Quaid-e-Azam 1876-1948 is buried in Karachi.
    Ans: Quaid-e-Azam (1876-1948) is buried in Karachi.

mcqs.q: Which sentence puts parentheses correctly around the amount, as in the book's example?
options: She paid a lot Rs. 5000 (for the cricket bat).
She paid a lot (Rs. 5000) for the cricket bat.
(She paid) a lot Rs. 5000 for the cricket bat.
She paid a lot Rs. (5000 for the cricket bat).
mcqs.why: The book's solved example encloses only the extra amount in parentheses: 'She paid a lot (Rs. 5000) for the cricket bat', leaving the rest of the sentence outside.

mcqs.q: His imprisonment lasted for four years 2002–2006. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: His imprisonment lasted for four years (2002–2006).
mcqs.why: The date range is the extra information, so it is enclosed: 'His imprisonment lasted for four years (2002–2006)', exactly as solved in the book.

mcqs.q: Quaid-e-Azam 1876-1948 is buried in Karachi. Which version is correct?
mcqs.why: The years of his life are supplemental information added after his name, so the book solves it as 'Quaid-e-Azam (1876-1948) is buried in Karachi.'

mcqs.q: He paid a small amount Rs. 800 for the cricket gloves. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: He paid a small amount Rs. 800 for (the cricket gloves).
(He paid) a small amount Rs. 800 for the cricket gloves.
He paid a small amount Rs. (800 for the cricket gloves).
He paid a small amount (Rs. 800) for the cricket gloves.
mcqs.why: Following the book's example with Rs. 5000, only the amount is extra information, so it alone goes inside parentheses: '(Rs. 800)'.

mcqs.q: Her training course lasted for two years 2021–2023. Which version is correct?
options: Her training course lasted for two years (2021–2023).
Her training (course lasted) for two years 2021–2023.
Her training course lasted for (two years) 2021–2023.
(Her training course lasted for two years) 2021–2023.
mcqs.why: Like the imprisonment sentence in the book, the years form a date range giving extra information about the length of time, so the range is put in parentheses.

mcqs.q: Ahmed spent a lot Rs. 1500 on his school books. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: Ahmed spent a lot Rs. 1500 on (his school books).
Ahmed spent a lot (Rs. 1500) on his school books.
(Ahmed spent) a lot Rs. 1500 on his school books.
Ahmed spent a lot Rs. (1500 on his school books).
mcqs.why: The amount Rs. 1500 is the supplemental detail, so, in the same style as the book's example, it is enclosed in parentheses and the rest of the sentence stays outside.

mcqs.q: The old man 1940-2020 lived in our village. Which version is correct?
options: The old man 1940-2020 lived in (our village).
(The old man) 1940-2020 lived in our village.
The old man (1940-2020) lived in our village.
The old man 1940-(2020 lived) in our village.
mcqs.why: Just as the years after Quaid-e-Azam's name are enclosed in the book, the life years after 'The old man' are extra information and belong in parentheses.

mcqs.q: She bought the football for a low price Rs. 600. Which version is correct?
options: She bought the football for a low price Rs. (600).
She (bought the football) for a low price Rs. 600.
She bought the football for a low price (Rs. 600).
She bought the football (for a low price) Rs. 600.
mcqs.why: The price is an amount added as extra information, so it is enclosed in parentheses at the place where it appears, following the pattern of the book's solved items.

mcqs.q: His stay at the workshop lasted for five years 2015–2020. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: His stay at the workshop lasted for five years (2015–2020).
His stay (at the workshop) lasted for five years 2015–2020.
His stay at the workshop lasted for (five years) 2015–2020.
(His stay at the workshop lasted) for five years 2015–2020.
mcqs.why: The years 2015–2020 are a date range giving extra information about the five years, so the whole range, and nothing else, is put inside parentheses.

mcqs.q: The teacher paid a lot Rs. 2000 for the story books. Which version is correct?
options: The teacher paid a lot Rs. 2000 (for the story books).
The teacher paid a lot (Rs. 2000) for the story books.
The teacher (paid a lot) Rs. 2000 for the story books.
The teacher paid a lot Rs. (2000 for the story) books.
mcqs.why: This follows the book's example exactly: the amount spent is supplemental information, so '(Rs. 2000)' is enclosed while the main sentence remains outside the brackets.

mcqs.q: Bilal 2010-2018 studied at the village school. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: Bilal (2010-2018) studied at the village school.
Bilal 2010-(2018 studied) at the village school.
mcqs.why: The years after a name, like 1876-1948 after Quaid-e-Azam in the book, are extra information about the person, so they are enclosed in parentheses after the name.

mcqs.q: They paid a huge amount Rs. 10000 for the carpet. Which version is correct?
options: They paid a huge amount Rs. (10000 for the carpet).
They (paid a huge) amount Rs. 10000 for the carpet.
They paid a huge (amount) Rs. 10000 for the carpet.
They paid a huge amount (Rs. 10000) for the carpet.
mcqs.why: Only the amount is extra information in this sentence, so '(Rs. 10000)' goes in parentheses, in the same style as '(Rs. 5000)' in the book's example.

mcqs.q: Her service in the school lasted for ten years 2012–2022. Which version is correct?
options: Her service in the school lasted for ten years (2012–2022).
Her service (in the school) lasted for ten years 2012–2022.
(Her service in the school lasted) for ten years 2012–2022.
Her service in the school lasted for (ten years) 2012–2022.
mcqs.why: The date range 2012–2022 adds extra information about the ten years of service, so the range is enclosed in parentheses, like '(2002–2006)' in the book.

mcqs.q: He gave me a small sum Rs. 250 for the gloves. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: He gave me a small sum Rs. (250 for the gloves).
He gave me a small sum (Rs. 250) for the gloves.
He (gave me) a small sum Rs. 250 for the gloves.
He gave me a small (sum) Rs. 250 for the gloves.
mcqs.why: The amount of the sum is the supplemental detail, so it is enclosed as '(Rs. 250)', keeping the opening and closing brackets around the amount only.

mcqs.q: The famous poet 1877-1938 wrote many poems. Which version is correct?
options: The famous poet 1877-(1938 wrote) many poems.
The famous poet (1877-1938) wrote many poems.
mcqs.why: The life years written after a person's name or title are extra information, so they are placed in parentheses, exactly as with Quaid-e-Azam (1876-1948) in the book.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — A. Mind map and short description of a child labourer

  • Q: A. Draw a mind map to give detailed imaginary physical description and personality traits of a child labourer. With the help of mind map write short description of the child labourer using basic connectors.
    Ans: Mind map (in words): In the centre write 'A Child Labourer'. Around it write: Age — about eight years old; Face — thin and tired, with sad eyes; Clothes — old, torn and dirty; Hands — rough and wounded from hard work; Work — works in a workshop/factory from morning till night; Feelings — sad, lonely, beaten by the manager when late; Wish — wants to go to school and have friends. Short description: The child labourer is a thin boy of about eight years. He wears old and torn clothes, and his face looks tired and sad. His hands are rough because he works in a workshop from five in the morning till nine at night. He is beaten by the manager if he is late, so he always feels afraid. However, he is hardworking and patient. Above all, he wishes to go to school like other children and have friends with whom he could exchange story books.

Writing — B. School Information Form of Zubair Khan

  • Q: B. Zubair Khan wishes to go to school. If his dream comes true and he goes to school, how will he fill in the school information form below? After effective discussion over his introduction, help him fill the form below.
    Ans: School Information Form (filled from Zubair Khan's introduction on page 169): Name of Student: Zubair Khan Date of Birth of Student: Not stated in his introduction (he tells us only that he is 8 years old) Name of School: Not stated — he does not go to school yet; he only wishes to go to school Address of School: Not stated (Zubair Khan lives in Peshawar) Class in which the student is in: Not stated — he has never been to school Nationality: Pakistani

mcqs.q: How old is the child labourer described in the mind map and short description?
mcqs.why: The mind map gives the child labourer's age as about eight years old, and the description begins, 'The child labourer is a thin boy of about eight years.'

mcqs.q: How are the child labourer's clothes described?
mcqs.why: The mind map lists his clothes as old, torn and dirty, and the short description repeats that he wears old and torn clothes.

mcqs.q: Why are the child labourer's hands rough?
options: Because he plays in the mud all day
Because he writes a lot at school
Because he washes dishes at home
Because he works hard in a workshop
mcqs.why: The description says his hands are rough because he works in a workshop from morning till night; the mind map calls them rough and wounded from hard work.

mcqs.q: From what time to what time does the child labourer work?
options: From five in the morning till nine at night
From nine in the morning till five in the evening
From seven in the morning till two in the afternoon
From six in the evening till midnight
mcqs.why: The short description states that he works in a workshop from five in the morning till nine at night, a very long working day for a small child.

mcqs.q: What happens to the child labourer if he is late for work?
options: He is beaten by the manager
He is sent back home kindly
mcqs.why: Both the mind map and the description say he is beaten by the manager when he is late, so he always feels afraid at work.

mcqs.q: What is the child labourer's greatest wish?
options: To earn a lot of money quickly
To become the manager of the workshop
To go to school and have friends
mcqs.why: Above all, he wishes to go to school like other children and have friends with whom he could exchange story books.

mcqs.q: Which pair of traits best describes the child labourer in the description?
mcqs.why: Although he feels sad and afraid, the description says, 'However, he is hardworking and patient,' showing his good qualities despite his hard life.

mcqs.q: What is Zubair Khan's nationality in his School Information Form?
mcqs.why: The filled School Information Form gives Zubair Khan's nationality as Pakistani, one of the few details his introduction actually states.

mcqs.q: In which city does Zubair Khan live?
mcqs.why: Zubair Khan's introduction says he lives in Peshawar, and the form notes that he lives in Peshawar although the school address is not stated.

mcqs.q: Why is Zubair Khan's date of birth not written in the form?
options: Because he has forgotten it completely
Because his introduction does not state it; he tells only that he is 8 years old
Because the form has no column for it
Because the school refused to record it
mcqs.why: The form explains that the date of birth is not stated in his introduction; Zubair tells us only that he is 8 years old, so nothing is invented for that column.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — Role play

  • Q: Role play: Make group of five students for role play. Each student will perform the role of Zubair Khan in front of the class and will introduce himself as Zubair Khan.
    Ans: Model introduction (as printed in the book): 'Hello! My name is Zubair Khan. I am 8 years old. I live in Peshawar. I began working in a motor mechanic workshop at the age of six. As a child I worked from five in the morning till nine at night. If I am late, the manager beats me. I wish I could also go to school like other children and have friends with whom I could exchange story books.' Each student in the group performs this introduction in turn, speaking in the first person as Zubair Khan, in a sad and hopeful tone.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. What is sowing?
    Ans: Sowing is the scattering of seed upon, in, or over the soil so that a crop may grow. In the poem, the farmer throws grains right and left over the field as he walks up and down it.
  • Q: Q2. Have you ever seen a farmer sow seeds?
    Ans: Model answer: Yes, I have seen a farmer sow seeds in the fields of my village. He walked up and down the field and threw the grains right and left with his hand, just as the father in the poem does.
  • Q: Q3. What if the farmers do not sow seeds?
    Ans: If the farmers do not sow seeds, no crop will grow in the fields. There will be no grain, no food for the people, and everyone will go hungry, because it is the sown grain that by and by bears the good crop.

Reading — Deduce the meaning of the following words

  • Q: Give the meaning of 'way' (deduced from the poem).
    Ans: way — the manner or method in which something is done; here, the way the father sows the seed ('This is the way my father sow').
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'field' (deduced from the poem).
    Ans: field — an open piece of land where crops are grown and where the farmer sows the grains.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'knows' (deduced from the poem).
    Ans: knows — understands and is sure of something; the father knows that the grains he throws will bear a good crop.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'fast' (deduced from the poem).
    Ans: fast — quickly, at a great speed ('Walking fast or walking slow').
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'slow' (deduced from the poem).
    Ans: slow — not fast; moving at a low speed, the opposite of fast.

Glossary

  • Q: Give the meaning of 'Sows'.
    Ans: to scatter seed upon, in, or over the soil
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'grains'.
    Ans: the fruit of certain grasses which furnish the chief food of man, as corn, wheat, rye, oats, etc.
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'throw'.
    Ans: to fling, cast, or hurl with a certain whirling motion of the arm
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'while'.
    Ans: a period of indeterminate length (usually short) marked by some action or condition
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'crop'.
    Ans: grain or other product of the field while standing
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'bear'.
    Ans: to produce
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'share'.
    Ans: a certain number of equal portions into which any property or invested capital is divided
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'care'.
    Ans: serious attention

Comprehension — A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How does a farmer throw grains?
    Ans: The farmer throws the grains right and left as he goes up and down the field. He walks fast or walks slow, and throws the grains here and there with care, repeating 'Sow Sow Sow' as he goes.
  • Q: Q2. What is the main idea of the poem?
    Ans: The main idea of the poem is the hard work of the farmer who sows seeds with care and with faith in the future: he throws the grains here and there knowing that by and by they will bear a good crop, in which all he loves will have a share.
  • Q: Q3. Write down the implied and explicit meanings of the poem.
    Ans: Explicit (clearly stated) meaning: The poem openly describes a farmer sowing seeds — he goes up and down the field, walking fast or slow, throwing the grains right and left, and expects a good crop from them. Implied (hidden) meaning: The poem suggests that hard work done with care and patience always bears fruit in the end, and that the farmer works not for himself alone but so that all he loves may have a share in the crop.
  • Q: Q4. Describe the character of farmer in your words.
    Ans: The farmer in the poem is hardworking, careful and hopeful. He goes up and down the field, walking fast or walking slow, and throws the grains with care. He is unselfish, because he sows so that all he loves will have a share in the good crop. He is also patient and full of faith, for he knows that the grains thrown here and there will by and by bear the good crop.
  • Q: Q5. Summarize the poem in your own words.
    Ans: In this poem, Eva Lovet describes her father sowing seeds in the field. He walks up and down the field, sometimes fast and sometimes slow, throwing the grains right and left with care. He knows that the grains thrown here and there will, by and by, grow into a good crop. He throws the grains lovingly so that all the people he loves may have a share in the crop. In short, the poem praises the farmer's hard work, care and hope.
  • Q: Q6. In what ways are farmers useful to us?
    Ans: Farmers are useful to us in many ways. They sow seeds and grow the crops — corn, wheat, rye and oats — which are the chief food of man. Without their hard work in the fields we would have no grain to eat. As the poem shows, the farmer throws the grains with care so that all he loves, and indeed all of us, may have a share in the good crop.

mcqs.q: What is sowing?
options: Watering the crop after it has grown
The scattering of seed upon, in, or over the soil so that a crop may grow
Cutting the ripe crop from the field
Selling the grain in the market
mcqs.why: Sowing is defined as the scattering of seed upon, in, or over the soil so that a crop may grow, which is what the father in the poem does with the grains.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'grains' mean?
options: The fruit of certain grasses which furnish the chief food of man, as corn, wheat, rye and oats
Pieces of dry soil in a field
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'grains' as the fruit of certain grasses which furnish the chief food of man, such as corn, wheat, rye and oats.

mcqs.q: In the poem, what does 'bear' mean in 'bear the good crop'?
mcqs.why: The glossary gives 'bear' as 'to produce', so the grains thrown here and there will by and by produce, or bear, a good crop.

mcqs.q: How does the farmer throw the grains in the poem?
options: He throws them all in one corner of the field
He throws them right and left as he goes up and down the field
He drops them only while standing still
He throws them into a river nearby
mcqs.why: The poem and its answers tell us the farmer goes up and down the field, walking fast or slow, and throws the grains right and left with care.

mcqs.q: What is the main idea of the poem 'Sow Sow Sow'?
options: A farmer sells his crop for a high price
A farmer works only for his own profit
The hard work of a farmer who sows with care and faith, knowing the grains will bear a good crop for all he loves
Children should throw grains for fun
mcqs.why: The main idea is the farmer's hard work done with care and faith in the future: the grains will bear a good crop in which all he loves will have a share.

mcqs.q: Which words best describe the farmer in the poem?
mcqs.why: The farmer is described as hardworking, careful and hopeful, and also unselfish and patient, because he sows so that all he loves may have a share in the crop.

mcqs.q: Who describes her father sowing seeds in this poem?
mcqs.why: The summary states that in this poem Eva Lovet describes her father sowing seeds in the field, walking up and down and throwing the grains right and left.

mcqs.q: What will happen if the farmers do not sow seeds?
options: The fields will grow crops by themselves
No crop will grow, there will be no food, and everyone will go hungry
People will eat more fruit instead
The rain will sow the seeds for them
mcqs.why: If farmers do not sow, no crop will grow in the fields; there will be no grain and no food for the people, because only the sown grain bears the good crop.

mcqs.q: In the poem, what does 'fast' mean in 'Walking fast or walking slow'?
options: Tied tightly so it cannot move
mcqs.why: The deduced meanings give 'fast' as quickly, at a great speed, and 'slow' as its opposite, moving at a low speed, in the line 'Walking fast or walking slow'.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'crop' mean?
options: Grain or other product of the field while standing
Rain that falls on the field
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'crop' as grain or other product of the field while standing, which is what the sown grains grow into by and by.

lessons.title: Sounds and Speaking
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary — A. Rhyming words; B. Verbs (first form to second form)

  • Q: A1. Find three rhyming words from the poem.
    Ans: Three rhyming words from the poem are: sow, slow and throw. The poem also has the rhyming sets goes / knows / throws and share / care, and here / there / bear.
  • Q: A2. Create three more rhyming words from the words found.
    Ans: Three more rhyming words created from the words found (sow, slow, throw) are: grow, flow and glow.
  • Q: B. Change the verb into its second form: sow (first form) → ______
    Ans: sowed
  • Q: B. Change the verb into its second form: go (first form) → ______
    Ans: went
  • Q: B. Change the verb into its second form: throw (first form) → ______
    Ans: threw
  • Q: B. Change the verb into its second form: know (first form) → ______
    Ans: knew

mcqs.q: Which three words from the poem rhyme with each other?
mcqs.why: The solved exercise names sow, slow and throw as three rhyming words from the poem; they all share the same ending sound.

mcqs.q: Which three NEW rhyming words were created from sow, slow and throw?
mcqs.why: The exercise creates grow, flow and glow as three more rhyming words from the set sow, slow and throw, because they end with the same sound.

mcqs.q: What is the second form of the verb 'sow'?
mcqs.why: The solved verb exercise gives the second form of 'sow' as 'sowed', so the farmer sowed the seed yesterday is the correct past-tense use.

mcqs.q: What is the second form of the verb 'go'?
mcqs.why: The second form of 'go' is the irregular form 'went', as given in the solved exercise: go (first form) becomes went (second form).

mcqs.q: What is the second form of the verb 'throw'?
mcqs.why: The exercise gives 'threw' as the second form of 'throw', an irregular change, just as the father threw the grains right and left.

mcqs.q: What is the second form of the verb 'know'?
mcqs.why: The second form of 'know' is 'knew': the father knew that the grains he threw would bear a good crop, as the solved exercise shows.

mcqs.q: Which set of words from the poem also rhymes?
mcqs.why: Besides sow, slow and throw, the poem also has the rhyming set goes, knows and throws, along with share, care and here, there, bear.

mcqs.q: Which pair of words from the poem rhymes with 'care'?
mcqs.why: The notes list the rhyming set share / care from the poem: the farmer throws the grains with care so that all he loves may have a share in the crop.

mcqs.q: Which word rhymes with 'here' and 'there' in the poem?
mcqs.why: The notes give the rhyming set here, there and bear, from the grains that the farmer throws here and there and that will bear the good crop.

mcqs.q: A farmer walked up and down the field yesterday. Which sentence uses the correct second form?
options: He throwed the grains right and left.
He sow the grains yesterday morning.
He went up and down and threw the grains.
He knowed the crop would be good.
mcqs.why: The correct second forms from the exercise are went (go) and threw (throw); 'throwed' and 'knowed' are wrong, and 'sow' is only the first form.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar — A. Write a simile against each situation

  • Q: Q1. Those two children don't like each other.
    Ans: They always fight like cats and dogs. (Done in the book.)
  • Q: Q2. He will get lung cancer if he's not careful.
    Ans: He smokes like a chimney.
  • Q: Q3. The boy is very lazy.
    Ans: He sits there like a bump on a log.
  • Q: Q4. We shouldn't waste time worrying.
    Ans: Time flies like an arrow.
  • Q: Q5. That girl won't harm anyone.
    Ans: She's as gentle as a lamb.
  • Q: Q6. She sings melodiously.
    Ans: She can sing like a nightingale.
  • Q: Q7. She doesn't eat much.
    Ans: She eats like a bird.
  • Q: Q8. She can't see through his wickedness.
    Ans: She is as innocent as a lamb.
  • Q: Q9. I have many things to do today.
    Ans: I'm as busy as a beaver.
  • Q: Q10. I want to do well in my examination.
    Ans: Then I can fly like an eagle.

Grammar — B. Match the statements in column A with the similes in column B

  • Q: Match: Be careful of the broken glass.
    Ans: It's as sharp as a knife.
  • Q: Match: Please water that plant.
    Ans: It's as dry as the desert.
  • Q: Match: Put on some warm gloves.
    Ans: Your hands are as cold as ice.
  • Q: Match: Go to the bathroom to clean you hands.
    Ans: They're as black as coal.
  • Q: Match: She has done a lot of makeup.
    Ans: She looks as white as a ghost.
  • Q: Match: My father taught me many things.
    Ans: He's as wise as an owl.
  • Q: Match: I have heard that story many times before.
    Ans: It's as old as the hills.
  • Q: Match: Did you scrub the floor?
    Ans: It's as clean as a whistle.
  • Q: Match: My brother can push a truck.
    Ans: He's as strong as a bull.
  • Q: Match: The boy could not find the book on the shelf.
    Ans: He is as blind as a bat.
  • Q: Match: This bedsheet is clean and smells good.
    Ans: It's as fresh as a daisy.

mcqs.q: Those two children don't like each other. Which simile fits this situation?
options: They always fight like cats and dogs.
mcqs.why: The book's solved simile for two children who do not like each other is 'They always fight like cats and dogs', because cats and dogs are famous for fighting.

mcqs.q: He will get lung cancer if he is not careful. Which simile fits?
options: He sits like a bump on a log.
mcqs.why: A person who smokes heavily and without care is compared to a chimney pouring out smoke, so the solved simile is 'He smokes like a chimney.'

mcqs.q: The boy is very lazy. Which simile fits him?
options: He is as busy as a beaver.
He can fly like an eagle.
He sits there like a bump on a log.
He fights like a cat and dog.
mcqs.why: A lazy boy who just sits doing nothing is compared to a bump on a log, a useless lump on a piece of wood, as solved in the book.

mcqs.q: We shouldn't waste time worrying. Which simile is used about time?
mcqs.why: The solved simile is 'Time flies like an arrow', reminding us that time passes very fast, so we should not waste it in worrying.

mcqs.q: That girl won't harm anyone. Which simile fits her?
options: She's as gentle as a lamb.
She's as busy as a beaver.
mcqs.why: A girl who will not harm anyone is 'as gentle as a lamb', because a lamb is a soft, harmless and gentle animal, as given in the book.

mcqs.q: She sings melodiously. Which simile fits her singing?
options: She can sing like a chimney.
She can sing like a nightingale.
She can sing like a bump on a log.
She can sing like an arrow.
mcqs.why: The nightingale is famous for its sweet, melodious song, so a girl who sings melodiously 'can sing like a nightingale', as solved in the book.

mcqs.q: She doesn't eat much. Which simile fits her?
mcqs.why: Birds eat very little at a time, so a girl who does not eat much 'eats like a bird', which is the simile given in the solved exercise.

mcqs.q: I have many things to do today. Which simile fits me?
options: I'm as gentle as a lamb.
I'm as innocent as a lamb.
I'm as busy as a beaver.
mcqs.why: A beaver is always busy working, so a person with many things to do is 'as busy as a beaver', the simile solved in the book for this situation.

mcqs.q: I want to do well in my examination. Which simile completes the wish: 'Then I can ______.'?
options: sit like a bump on a log
mcqs.why: The book solves this as 'Then I can fly like an eagle', picturing the high success of doing well in the examination like an eagle flying high.

mcqs.q: Be careful of the broken glass. Which simile matches this warning?
options: It's as dry as the desert.
It's as sharp as a knife.
It's as old as the hills.
It's as fresh as a daisy.
mcqs.why: Broken glass can cut like a blade, so the matching simile in the exercise is 'It's as sharp as a knife', which explains why we must be careful.

mcqs.q: Please water that plant. Which simile shows why it needs water?
options: It's as clean as a whistle.
It's as strong as a bull.
It's as dry as the desert.
It's as white as a ghost.
mcqs.why: The plant needs water because 'It's as dry as the desert', the matching simile in the exercise; a desert is the driest place we know.

mcqs.q: Put on some warm gloves. Which simile matches this advice?
options: Your hands are as black as coal.
Your hands are as fresh as a daisy.
Your hands are as wise as an owl.
Your hands are as cold as ice.
mcqs.why: Warm gloves are advised because 'Your hands are as cold as ice', the simile matched to this statement in the book's exercise.

mcqs.q: My father taught me many things. Which simile describes him?
options: He's as wise as an owl.
He's as blind as a bat.
He's as strong as a bull.
mcqs.why: The owl stands for wisdom, so a father who taught many things is 'as wise as an owl', as matched in the solved exercise.

mcqs.q: My brother can push a truck. Which simile describes him?
options: He's as gentle as a lamb.
He's as strong as a bull.
He's as dry as the desert.
He's as clean as a whistle.
mcqs.why: Only great strength can push a truck, and the book matches this with 'He's as strong as a bull', because a bull is a very powerful animal.

mcqs.q: Did you scrub the floor? Which simile praises the clean floor?
options: It's as old as the hills.
It's as clean as a whistle.
It's as white as a ghost.
mcqs.why: A well-scrubbed floor is 'as clean as a whistle', the simile matched in the exercise to the question about scrubbing the floor.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Rewrite the story with a new ending

  • Q: Rewrite the story that you discussed in 'Listening and Speaking' with new ending in your notebooks.
    Ans: The Brave Firefighters (rewritten with a new ending): One day a house in our street caught fire and tall flames rose from its roof. We ran out and someone telephoned the fire brigade. Within minutes the fire engine arrived, and the brave firefighters climbed up their ladders and sprayed water on the fire. After a hard struggle the flames died down, but the house was badly burnt and the family had lost many of their things. New ending: The neighbours did not leave the family alone. Everyone in the street collected money, food and clothes for them, and the workmen rebuilt the house within a few weeks. On the day the family returned to their home, they thanked the firefighters and the neighbours, and the children of the street promised never to play with fire again.

mcqs.q: In the rewritten story 'The Brave Firefighters', what caught fire one day?
mcqs.why: The story begins with a house in our street catching fire, with tall flames rising from its roof, before the fire brigade is telephoned.

mcqs.q: From where did tall flames rise in the story?
options: From the roof of the house
From a tree near the house
mcqs.why: The rewritten story says tall flames rose from the roof of the house that had caught fire in the street.

mcqs.q: How did the fire brigade reach the burning house so quickly?
options: Someone telephoned the fire brigade and the fire engine arrived within minutes
The firefighters were already living in the house
A neighbour carried water in buckets only
The rain put the fire out first
mcqs.why: In the story, someone telephoned the fire brigade, and within minutes the fire engine arrived with the brave firefighters.

mcqs.q: What did the brave firefighters do to fight the fire?
options: They watched the flames from far away
They climbed up their ladders and sprayed water on the fire
They broke all the windows of the house
They asked the family to leave the street
mcqs.why: The firefighters climbed up their ladders and sprayed water on the fire, and after a hard struggle the flames died down.

mcqs.q: What was the condition of the house after the fire was put out?
options: It was badly burnt and the family had lost many of their things
mcqs.why: The story says that after the flames died down, the house was badly burnt and the family had lost many of their things.

mcqs.q: In the NEW ending, how did the neighbours help the family?
options: They collected money, food and clothes for them
They only sent them good wishes
They built a shop for them
mcqs.why: The new ending says the neighbours did not leave the family alone; everyone in the street collected money, food and clothes for them.

mcqs.q: In the new ending, who rebuilt the house, and how soon?
options: The firefighters rebuilt it in one day
The family rebuilt it alone in a year
The workmen rebuilt it within a few weeks
mcqs.why: In the new ending, the workmen rebuilt the house within a few weeks, and the family was able to return to their home.

mcqs.q: Whom did the family thank on the day they returned to their home?
options: Only the children of the street
mcqs.why: On the day the family returned home, they thanked the firefighters and the neighbours who had helped them in their trouble.

mcqs.q: What did the children of the street promise in the new ending?
options: To telephone the fire brigade every day
Never to play with fire again
mcqs.why: The new ending closes with the children of the street promising never to play with fire again, having seen the damage fire can do.

mcqs.q: What is the title of the rewritten story?
mcqs.why: The story discussed and rewritten with a new ending is titled 'The Brave Firefighters', after the men who fought the house fire.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — A. Guess the story from the pictures

  • Q: A. Work in pairs and guess the story (from the pictures). Give the story a title. Share your views with the class.
    Ans: Model story — Title: 'The Brave Firefighters'. One day a house caught fire and flames began to rise from its roof. Someone at once telephoned the fire brigade, and a fireman took the call. The fire engine rushed to the spot with its crew. The firefighters climbed up ladders and sprayed water on the flames until the fire was put out. The house was badly burnt and black smoke was still rising from it, but luckily the family was safe. In the last picture, workmen are seen repairing and rebuilding the damaged house. Share these views with the class and discuss the characters and the moral of helping others in danger.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Look at the pictures and predict the theme of the lesson.
    Ans: The pictures show red tents pitched on green ground under high, snow-covered mountains, and a beautiful valley town in Swat. So the theme of the lesson can be predicted before reading: it is about a camping holiday — a scout troop's camp in the Swat valley.

Glossary

  • Q: Give the meaning of 'camping'.
    Ans: the act of encamping and living in tents in a camp
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'bank'.
    Ans: a mound, pile, or ridge of earth, raised above the surrounding level (in the lesson, the side of the river — 'On the right bank of the river')
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'slope'.
    Ans: any ground whose surface forms an angle with the place of the horizon
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'plentiful'.
    Ans: existing in great number or quantity
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'troop'.
    Ans: a unit of girl or boy scouts
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'delighted'.
    Ans: greatly pleased
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'scattered'.
    Ans: move away from each other
  • Q: Give the meaning of 'appetite'.
    Ans: desire for food or drink; hunger

Comprehension — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Why did the Pak Pioneers send an advance party to Swat?
    Ans: The Pak Pioneers sent an advance party to Swat District in order to choose the place for the camp, because all camping holidays have to be carefully planned, especially when visiting a place like Swat. Tahir and Kamal were chosen to do this.
  • Q: Q2. What did the troop do after dinner?
    Ans: After dinner the troop sat round the camp fire and sang songs for half an hour. Then the leader prepared a programme of activities for the rest of the holidays.
  • Q: Q3. How did the troop get to Madyan?
    Ans: The troop got to Madyan by bus. The scout hired a bus which took them and all their equipment to Madyan.
  • Q: Q4. What do you mean by DOING A GOOD TURN?
    Ans: 'Doing a good turn' means taking every opportunity of helping other people. Like all good scouts, the Pak Pioneers call this helping of others DOING A GOOD TURN.
  • Q: Q5. How far did the scouts walk on the second day?
    Ans: On the walk described in the lesson the scouts walked to Bahrain, which is about ten kilometres from Madyan. They walked at a good speed and reached Bahrain in about an hour and a half.
  • Q: Q6. Where is Bahrain situated?
    Ans: Bahrain is a village situated where river Swat and the river Daral meet. The sources of the river Swat are about sixty-nine kilometres beyond Bahrain.
  • Q: Q7. Why did the scouts think that the bear had climbed up the tree?
    Ans: The scouts followed the tracks for several hundred metres and then the tracks seemed to stop, and they could find no more marks on the ground. So one of the boys said, 'The bear must have climbed a tree.' They examined the trunks of the neighbouring trees and on one of them they saw a fresh mark of a bear's claws, and looking up, they saw a small mountain bear sitting on a branch about six metres above them.
  • Q: Q8. How many 'good turns' did the scouts do on their GOOD TURN MARCH?
    Ans: The scouts did two good turns on their GOOD TURN march: (1) they helped a little boy to mend his fishing line, and (2) they moved some rocks that had fallen across the road.
  • Q: Q9. What places of special interest did the scouts visit?
    Ans: Before the troop left Swat, they visited the White Palace of the Badshah Jan at Marghazar and some of the Buddhist remains at Butkada near Mingora, for which the district is famous.

mcqs.q: What does 'camping' mean?
options: Travelling by bus to a town
The act of encamping and living in tents in a camp
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'camping' as the act of encamping and living in tents in a camp, which is what the scout troop does in the Swat valley.

mcqs.q: What is a 'troop' in this lesson?
options: A group of soldiers in a war
A unit of girl or boy scouts
mcqs.why: The glossary gives 'troop' as a unit of girl or boy scouts, and the lesson is about the Pak Pioneers scout troop camping in Swat.

mcqs.q: Why did the Pak Pioneers send an advance party to Swat?
options: To catch fish in the river Swat
To choose the place for the camp, because camping holidays must be carefully planned
To visit the White Palace first
To buy food for the whole troop
mcqs.why: The advance party was sent to choose the place for the camp, because all camping holidays have to be carefully planned, especially when visiting a place like Swat.

mcqs.q: Who were chosen for the advance party to Swat?
options: The troop leader and a cook
mcqs.why: The notes name Tahir and Kamal as the two scouts chosen to go ahead to Swat and choose the place for the camp.

mcqs.q: What did the troop do after dinner at the camp?
options: They went straight to sleep in their tents
They sat round the camp fire and sang songs for half an hour
They walked to Bahrain in the dark
They packed their bags to go home
mcqs.why: After dinner the troop sat round the camp fire and sang songs for half an hour, and then the leader prepared a programme of activities for the holidays.

mcqs.q: How did the troop get to Madyan?
options: By a hired bus that took them and all their equipment
By boat down the river Swat
mcqs.why: The troop got to Madyan by bus: the scout hired a bus which took them and all their equipment to Madyan.

mcqs.q: What do the Pak Pioneers mean by 'DOING A GOOD TURN'?
options: Turning round quickly on a march
Taking every opportunity of helping other people
Cooking a meal for the troop
mcqs.why: Like all good scouts, the Pak Pioneers call taking every opportunity of helping other people 'DOING A GOOD TURN'.

mcqs.q: How far is Bahrain from Madyan, and how long did the scouts take to walk there?
options: About ten kilometres, reached in about an hour and a half
About two kilometres, reached in ten minutes
About sixty-nine kilometres, reached in a full day
About five kilometres, reached in three hours
mcqs.why: The scouts walked to Bahrain, which is about ten kilometres from Madyan, walking at a good speed and reaching it in about an hour and a half.

mcqs.q: Where is Bahrain situated?
options: On the top of a snow-covered mountain
Near the Buddhist remains at Butkada
Where river Swat and the river Daral meet
Beside the White Palace at Marghazar
mcqs.why: Bahrain is a village situated where river Swat and the river Daral meet, and the sources of the river Swat are about sixty-nine kilometres beyond it.

mcqs.q: Which two good turns did the scouts do on their GOOD TURN march?
options: They sang songs and cooked dinner
They helped a little boy mend his fishing line and moved rocks that had fallen across the road
They pitched tents and lit a camp fire
They visited a palace and some old remains
mcqs.why: The scouts did two good turns on the march: they helped a little boy to mend his fishing line, and they moved some rocks that had fallen across the road.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary — A. Word meanings and parts of speech; B. Direct quotations; C. Syllables

  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'pioneer'.
    Ans: Meaning: a person who is one of the first to explore, settle or develop a new area or activity (in the lesson, a member of the Pak Pioneers scout troop). Part of speech: Noun.
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'load'.
    Ans: Meaning: a quantity or burden that is carried or put on something; as a verb, to put a load on something. Part of speech: Noun (also used as a Verb).
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'climbed'.
    Ans: Meaning: went up something, especially using the hands and feet ('The bear must have climbed a tree'). Part of speech: Verb (past tense of 'climb').
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'amused'.
    Ans: Meaning: entertained and made to enjoy oneself ('others just walked along the river bank and amused themselves'). Part of speech: Verb (past tense of 'amuse').
  • Q: Give the meaning and part of speech of 'journey'.
    Ans: Meaning: a long trip or travelling from one place to another ('tired after their long journey'). Part of speech: Noun.
  • Q: B. Find and underline the direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the text.
    Ans: The direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks in the text are: (1) 'The bear must have climbed a tree.' and (2) 'GOOD TURN' (in 'a "GOOD TURN" march').
  • Q: C. Words with 1 syllable (from the box: special, cook, bear, tree, trip, troop, advance, good, delighted, appetite, slope, bank, scattered, situated, supplies)
    Ans: 1 syllable: cook, bear, tree, trip, troop, good, slope, bank
  • Q: C. Words with 2 syllables
    Ans: 2 syllables: special (spe-cial), advance (ad-vance), scattered (scat-tered), supplies (sup-plies)
  • Q: C. Words with 3 syllables
    Ans: 3 syllables: delighted (de-light-ed), appetite (ap-pe-tite). Note: 'situated' has four syllables (sit-u-at-ed), so it does not fit any of the three columns printed in the book.

Grammar — Conditional Sentences (Type I): A. Choose the correct option; B. Complete with the correct form

  • Q: Q1. If you study hard, you ______ the exam.
    Options: passed / will pass / pass
    Ans: will pass
  • Q: Q2. I will go the party if ______ time.
    Options: I had / I will have / I have
    Ans: I have
  • Q: Q3. If we ______ the game, we ______.
    Options: win/will celebrate / win/will win / will win/celebrate
    Ans: win/will celebrate
  • Q: Q4. What ______ if it rains?
    Options: did you do / do you do / will you do
    Ans: will you do
  • Q: Q5. If the weather ______ good, I ______ tennis.
    Options: will be/will play / was/played / is/will play
    Ans: is/will play
  • Q: B1. Complete: If I ______ (go) out tonight, I ______ (go) to the cinema.
    Ans: If I go out tonight, I will go to the cinema.
  • Q: B2. Complete: If you ______ (get) back late, I ______ (be) angry.
    Ans: If you get back late, I will be angry.
  • Q: B3. Complete: If we ______ (not/see) each other tomorrow, we ______ (see) each other next week.
    Ans: If we do not see each other tomorrow, we will see each other next week.
  • Q: B4. Complete: If he ______ (come), I ______ (be) surprised.
    Ans: If he comes, I will be surprised.
  • Q: B5. Complete: If we ______ (wait) here, we ______ (be) late.
    Ans: If we wait here, we will be late.

Grammar — Second Conditional Sentences (Type II): A. Complete with the correct form; B. Choose the correct form of the verb

  • Q: A1. Complete: If I ______ (be) you, I ______ (get) a new job.
    Ans: If I were you, I would get a new job.
  • Q: A2. Complete: If he ______ (be) younger, he ______ (travel) more.
    Ans: If he were younger, he would travel more.
  • Q: A3. Complete: If we ______ (not/be) friends, I ______ (be) angry with you.
    Ans: If we were not friends, I would be angry with you.
  • Q: A4. Complete: If I ______ (have) enough money, I ______ (buy) a big house.
    Ans: If I had enough money, I would buy a big house.
  • Q: A5. Complete: If she ______ (not/be) always so late, she ______ (be) promoted.
    Ans: If she were not always so late, she would be promoted.
  • Q: B1. We don't mind camping, but if we ______ enough money, we ______ in a hotel.
    Options: have... stayed / had... would stay / had... stayed / would have...stayed
    Ans: had... would stay
  • Q: B2. He's so stupid! If he ______ an animal, he would be a sheep.
    Options: would be / was / were / are
    Ans: were
  • Q: B3. If there ______ no mosquitos, there would be no malaria.
    Options: were / are / would be / is
    Ans: were
  • Q: B4. If her hair were black, she ______ completely different.
    Options: looks / look / will look / would look
    Ans: would look
  • Q: B5. If he were a young man, he ______ able to walk faster.
    Options: is / would be / was / will be
    Ans: would be

Revision Unit 16-19 — A. Conditional Sentences (Type I); B. Conditional Sentences (Type II); C. Parentheses

  • Q: A1. Complete: If you (send) ______ this letter now, she (receive) ______ it tomorrow.
    Ans: If you send this letter now, she will receive it tomorrow.
  • Q: A2. Complete: If I (do) ______ this test, I (improve) ______ my English.
    Ans: If I do this test, I will improve my English.
  • Q: A3. Complete: If I (find) ______ your ring, I (give) ______ it back to you.
    Ans: If I find your ring, I will give it back to you.
  • Q: A4. Complete: Rasheed (go) ______ shopping if she (have) ______ time in the afternoon.
    Ans: Rasheed will go shopping if she has time in the afternoon.
  • Q: A5. Complete: Saima (go) ______ to London next week if he (get) ______ a cheap flight.
    Ans: Saima will go to London next week if he gets a cheap flight. (Pronouns as printed in the book.)
  • Q: B1. Complete: If I (have) ______ more time, I (learn) ______ to play the guitar.
    Ans: If I had more time, I would learn to play the guitar.
  • Q: B2. Complete: If she (study) ______ harder, she (get) ______ better marks.
    Ans: If she studied harder, she would get better marks.
  • Q: B3. Complete: If we (know) ______ more about history, we (be / not) ______ afraid of the test.
    Ans: If we knew more about history, we would not be afraid of the test.
  • Q: B4. Complete: I (go) ______ jogging with Tania and Sumaira if they (be) ______ here this week.
    Ans: I would go jogging with Tania and Sumaira if they were here this week.
  • Q: B5. Complete: It (surprise) ______ me if she (help / not) ______ you.
    Ans: It would surprise me if she did not help you.
  • Q: C1. Use parentheses where needed: I'll get back to you tomorrow Friday.
    Ans: I'll get back to you tomorrow (Friday).
  • Q: C2. Use parentheses where needed: Which country countries do you want to visit?
    Ans: Which country (countries) do you want to visit?
  • Q: C3. Use parentheses where needed: You put fifty-four 54 books on that shelf.
    Ans: You put fifty-four (54) books on that shelf.
  • Q: C4. Use parentheses where needed: We are going to visit Brazil I don't know where this spring.
    Ans: We are going to visit Brazil (I don't know where) this spring.
  • Q: C5. Use parentheses where needed: To take this ride, you need to 1 shut your eyes, 2 hang on tight, and 3 pray.
    Ans: To take this ride, you need to (1) shut your eyes, (2) hang on tight, and (3) pray.

Revision Unit 16-19 — D. Insert similes to complete the sentences

  • Q: Is there anything to eat? I'm as hungry as a ______.
    Ans: horse
  • Q: It hasn't rained for months — the ground's as dry as a ______.
    Ans: bone
  • Q: You'll have to speak up when you're with Tahir; he's as deaf as a ______.
    Ans: post
  • Q: Masood was so embarrassed when we found out he was lying; his face was as red as a ______.
    Ans: beetroot
  • Q: I can't see a thing without my glasses. I'm as blind as a ______.
    Ans: bat
  • Q: Your brother's as thin as a ______. Is he eating enough?
    Ans: rake
  • Q: I promise I won't wake you up when I get home. I'll be as quiet as a ______.
    Ans: mouse
  • Q: This bag's not heavy — it's as light as a ______.
    Ans: feather

mcqs.q: If you study hard, you ______ the exam.
mcqs.why: This is a Type I conditional from the book: a present-tense if-clause takes 'will' in the main clause, so 'you will pass the exam' is correct.

mcqs.q: I will go to the party if ______ time.
mcqs.why: In a Type I conditional the if-clause uses the present simple, so the book's answer is 'I have': 'I will go to the party if I have time.'

mcqs.q: If we ______ the game, we ______.
mcqs.why: The book's correct pair is 'win / will celebrate': present simple after 'if' and 'will' plus the base verb in the result clause of a Type I conditional.

mcqs.q: What ______ if it rains?
mcqs.why: For a possible future condition, the book's answer is 'will you do': 'What will you do if it rains?' follows the Type I pattern.

mcqs.q: If the weather ______ good, I ______ tennis.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is 'is / will play': the if-clause takes the present simple 'is' and the main clause takes 'will play' in a Type I conditional.

mcqs.q: If I ______ you, I ______ a new job. (Type II)
mcqs.why: This Type II conditional is unreal, so the book uses 'were' for all persons and 'would get': 'If I were you, I would get a new job.'

mcqs.q: If I ______ enough money, I ______ a big house. (Type II)
mcqs.why: In the Type II pattern the if-clause takes the past simple 'had' and the main clause takes 'would buy', as solved in the book.

mcqs.q: We don't mind camping, but if we ______ enough money, we ______ in a hotel.
mcqs.why: The book's chosen option is 'had... would stay', the Type II form, because staying in a hotel is an unreal wish against the fact that they are camping.

mcqs.q: If he ______ an animal, he would be a sheep.
mcqs.why: With 'would be' in the main clause, the if-clause needs the Type II form 'were', which is used for every person: 'If he were an animal...'

mcqs.q: If there ______ no mosquitos, there would be no malaria.
mcqs.why: The main clause 'there would be no malaria' shows a Type II conditional, so the book's answer for the if-clause is 'were'.

mcqs.q: What part of speech is 'pioneer' in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The vocabulary exercise gives 'pioneer' as a noun: a person who is one of the first to explore, settle or develop a new area or activity, here a member of the Pak Pioneers.

mcqs.q: 'Climbed' in 'The bear must have climbed a tree' is:
options: A verb, the past tense of 'climb'
mcqs.why: The exercise explains that 'climbed' is a verb, the past tense of 'climb', meaning went up something using the hands and feet.

mcqs.q: How many syllables are there in the word 'delighted'?
mcqs.why: The syllable exercise puts 'delighted' in the three-syllable column as de-light-ed, like 'appetite' (ap-pe-tite) in the same list.

mcqs.q: How many syllables are there in the word 'situated'?
options: Three syllables, as printed in the book's columns
mcqs.why: Counted correctly, 'situated' has four syllables, sit-u-at-ed, so it does not fit any of the book's three columns; the notes point out this misfit in the printed exercise.

mcqs.q: You put fifty-four 54 books on that shelf. Where do the parentheses belong?
options: You put fifty-four 54 (books on that shelf).
You put (fifty-four) 54 books on that shelf.
You put fifty-four (54) books on that shelf.
(You put fifty-four 54 books) on that shelf.
mcqs.why: In the revision exercise the number in figures is extra information added after the number in words, so it is enclosed: 'fifty-four (54) books'.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Paragraph: 'If I were the principal of my school'

  • Q: Write an imaginary paragraph on the topic 'If I were the principal of my school', keeping in mind conventions of paragraph writing and first and second conditional sentences.
    Ans: If I were the principal of my school, I would make my school the best school in the whole district. If the students worked hard, they would win prizes in every examination. I would build a big library, and if a student had no money for books, I would give him books free of cost. If the teachers needed training, I would arrange special classes for them. I would plant trees all around the school, and if the playground were bigger, the students would play more games. I would start a scout troop like the Pak Pioneers, and if the weather were fine, we would go on a camping holiday to Swat. If any student were poor, I would help him from the school fund. In short, if I were the principal, I would make the school a place where every child loves to learn.

mcqs.q: In the paragraph 'If I were the principal of my school', what would the writer make his school?
options: The biggest school in the city only
The best school in the whole district
A school only for rich students
mcqs.why: The paragraph begins: 'If I were the principal of my school, I would make my school the best school in the whole district.'

mcqs.q: What would happen if the students worked hard, in the writer's plan?
options: They would win prizes in every examination
They would leave the school early
They would play games all day
mcqs.why: The writer says, 'If the students worked hard, they would win prizes in every examination,' using a conditional sentence in the paragraph.

mcqs.q: What building would the principal add to the school?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says, 'I would build a big library,' so that students can read and learn more in the school.

mcqs.q: What would the principal do if a student had no money for books?
options: He would send the student home
He would give him books free of cost
mcqs.why: The writer promises: 'if a student had no money for books, I would give him books free of cost,' showing kindness to poor students.

mcqs.q: What would the principal arrange if the teachers needed training?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says, 'If the teachers needed training, I would arrange special classes for them,' so that teaching in the school improves.

mcqs.q: What would the principal plant all around the school?
options: Flower pots only in the office
mcqs.why: The writer says, 'I would plant trees all around the school,' making the school green and pleasant for the students.

mcqs.q: What would the students do if the playground were bigger?
options: They would study in the playground
They would leave the school sooner
mcqs.why: The paragraph uses the conditional: 'if the playground were bigger, the students would play more games,' linking a bigger ground with more play.

mcqs.q: What troop would the principal start, and like whom?
options: A cricket team like the school eleven
A scout troop like the Pak Pioneers
A music band like the village band
A debating society like the town club
mcqs.why: The writer says, 'I would start a scout troop like the Pak Pioneers,' the scout troop from the camping lesson in Swat.

mcqs.q: Where would the school go on a camping holiday if the weather were fine?
mcqs.why: The paragraph says, 'if the weather were fine, we would go on a camping holiday to Swat,' following the Pak Pioneers' example.

mcqs.q: How would the principal help a poor student, in the paragraph's plan?
options: He would help him from the school fund
He would ask other students for money
He would excuse him from all lessons
mcqs.why: The writer promises, 'If any student were poor, I would help him from the school fund,' so that poverty does not stop his learning.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — What would you take on a camping trip?

  • Q: Make groups of five students each and think about what you would take on a camping trip. Provide the following sentence: I would pack ______ because ______. After brainstorming, share your ideas with the class.
    Ans: Model answers: 'I would pack a warm coat because it may rain and turn cold in Swat, as each scout in the lesson carried a small pack containing food and a coat in case of rain.' 'I would pack food and a water bottle because a plentiful supply of food is needed on the journey.' 'I would pack a torch and matches because the camp needs fire and light at night.' Each group member gives one such sentence and, after brainstorming, shares his ideas with the class.
